speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister or Militia and Defence).
speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I desire to refer to a matter which I think is of sufficient importance to be brought to the attention of the House ; that is, the fact that a Canadian, Private Perry, of Vancouver, B.C., has won the King's prize at Bisley camp. Private Perry, I believe, is the first Canadian-born soldier who has won this prize, although this prize was brought to Canada once before ; it was then brought by a citizen of Canada, but not by a man who had been born in this country. Private Perry also served with distinction in South Africa. I had the honour of sending a cablegram, as soon as the news reached Canada, to Private Perry through the commandant of the Bisley team, congratulating him upon his success. I am sure that this is a matter for congratulation upon the part of the militia of this country, on the part of this parliament and on the part of the people of Can ada generally.

I can heartily endorse, on behalf of the opposition, the statements that have been made by the Minister of Militia, and I may say that I feel proud to know that the former winner of the King's prize was a Canadian citizen, even if he were not a Canadian born. I am not aware that it makes a difference whether a Canadian is born within the bounds of the Dominion or not, so long as he is a good Canadian citizen. We welcome all, they are

not strangers to this country, so long as they become good Canadian citizens. I was a little surprised to see the minister make that distinction.
Oh, get out.
Mr. Perry is an old Toronto boy, and has reflected credit on the militia force, both as a member of the Royal Grenadiers of Toronto, of the South Africa corps and of our Bisley rifle team.

How frequent is the service ?
Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT, There are three routes : Route A, from Mulgrave to Canso ; route B, from Mulgrave to Guys-borough ; route C, from Port Mulgrave to Chgticamp, calling at Port Hastings, Mar-garee and Cheticamp Harbour. This is a service of great importance to those who are engaged in the fishing industry in Canso, and I have had a communication on the subject from persons who have undertaken the business of forwarding fresh fish to Ontario via the Intercolonial, and who complain to me that in the case, I think, of at least fifty per cent of the shipments during one season, the boat failed to make connection with the train at Mulgrave ; I am not absolutely sure of the percentage, but to the best of my recollection it amounted to that. The result was that the fish were detained for twenty-four hours, persons who were to be supplied in Montreal and Ontario were disappointed, and of course there was a deterioration of the goods to be forwarded. I think some effort should be made to have that service improved in that regard. I understand thoroughly that there are perils of the sea and difficulties of navigation which have to be taken into consideration, but it would be better to have an improved class of boats and give them more subsidy rather than to have so important a business as that to which I have referred, injured and possibly destroyed altogether. The hon. gentleman is of course aware, as is every one in the business, that in order to carry on the business of supplying fresh fish they must be enabled to guarantee a certain supply daily to Montreal or to any other place to which fish are to be forwarded. If you cannot guarantee that, through lack of good communication or by

reason of an insufficient supply of fish being brought in by the fishermen, the result will be that the trade will go somewhere else. For example, the gentleman to whom I refer, who is largely engaged in this business at Canso, said that a certain fish dealer in Toronto told him that he would give him an order for only one-third of what he required daily, but he added, I would be willing to give you an order one-half or two-thirds if I were sure the supply of fish would be adequate, and if your means of communication were absolutely certain. I believe the supply of fish is getting better and better. Those who are engaged in the business are sending out more fishermen, some of them to one part of the coast, others to other parts of the coast, so that from one source or another the proper supply of fish will be brought in, and that part of the business seems to be put upon a fairly good basis. The other part, adequate communication, seems to be still lacking. Of course that may be supplied if certain railway lines now projected in the province of Nova Scotia are constructed at an early date. However, in the meantime we have to depend on a service of this kind, and it is of exceeding importance that that service should be made reliable, otherwise this business cannot be carried on.

I quite agree with my hon. friend that it is not merely a desirable thing in itself, but it is of great importance as a feeder to the Intercolonial. My hon. friend is perhaps aware, as I am, of the difficulty we have had in getting decent fish supplied in Ottawa, and I should be glad to contribute as far as possible towards improving the service so that we may get fresh fish daily supplied to our breakfast tables in the west. I may say that we have altered the route with the purpose of helping this, Arichat is now dropped, and another service was authorized last session from Petit de Grat to Mulg;rave that enables us to effect a great improvement. I understand from my deputy we had a good many complaints last year, but this present year the service has been better, and the complaints have ceased. However, I entirely agree, for every reason, both for the encouragement of the fishermen, for the benefit of the Intercolonial and for the supply of the western provinces, that it is highly desirable that all reasonable assistance should be given.

I hope the minister will go a step further and urge upon his colleagues the support of the proposal I have made to put the express companies under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission so that their express charges may be regulated. In that way good will be accomplished, both in promoting interprovincial *trade and the fresh fish of the maritime provinces and in the fruit of the west. Nothing will prevent an interchange of that
trade so much as jurisdiction vested in the Railway Commission to control the rates of the express companies.

I am of the opinion that any improvement in that direction, on a large scale at least, would have to come from the railway companies themselves, through arrangements with the express agencies. My hon. friend is probably aware that the two great express agencies, the Canadian Company and the Dominion Company, are both parts and parcels of their respective railroads ; the Grand Trunk completely controls the one, and the Canadian Pacific Railway controls the other. as to the vexed question of meddling with the express rates, I would rather not enter on that controversy just now.
But it is an essential part of the issue.

It must be done by the action of the Intercolonial, and the Grand Trunk Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I should hope they might be able to see their way to run a fish train daily, as is done in some portions of the United States, through and through. I see no reason at all why a fish train should not be run from Nova Scotia or from the lower St. Lawrence, at any rate, as far as Toronto. I have more than once spoken of it and recommended it, and I will do so again.

In this connection I may say that I brought to the attention of the House the other day the fact that upon the Intercolonial Railway only one express company is permitted to carry on business. I think my hon. friend from Toronto suggested that another company applying was to be regarded as guilty of impertinence because it insisted upon having absolute control of the business upon the line of the railway company with which it is associated. Still I do not know that this conduct should be regarded as more impertinent than that the company, retaining control of the railway which it happens to be associated, should also desire to have complete control of the Intercolonial. However, that may be, the object of my suggestion would be amply met if we could have applied to the Intercolonial a provision which I find in the Railway Act with regard to express companies, and it is found in section 278.
Every company which grants any facilities for the carriage of goods by express to any incorporated express company or persons, shall grant equal facilities, on equal terms and conditions, to any other incorporated express company which demands the same.
The difficulty about the Intercolonial Railway is that that provision does not at the present time apply to it. It may be that section 278 is not very fully carried out by the great lines of this country which

have express companies connected with them. But nevertheless there is a law which apparently is capable of being carried out and if it were done under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission it night possibly- though there may be unexpected difficulties-afford. some of the relief by way of competition which has been advocated very forcibly by several hon. gentlemen in the House.

This clause has been appealed to on former occasions and it has not proved efficacious. As a matter of fact what I said before is true that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, notwithstanding this clause, have resisted any attempt on the part of express companies other than their own favourite companies which they own themselves to get upon their systems.
Can they successfully do that ?

Yes, one of the greatest lawsuits that has been tried and one in which the greatest amount of money has been spent was undertaken in an effort to force the Grand Trunk Railway Company to allow a rival express company, organized in the city of Toronto, to share the business of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The express company employed the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy, an immense amount of money was expended, but finally the rival company was beaten out. In connection with the Intercolonial Railway my idea is that this government should have a first-class express system upon its own road and that it should undertake to provide for express business in fish and other trade as between the maritime provinces and the west. I take the 'ground that the Intercolonial Railway should not be given over to two rival express companies unless the railway companies owning the express companies are prepared to grant the same pri-villege which they enjoy on their respective lines and unless in some way provision is made for the loss of revenue that would be entailed upon the Intercolonial Railway according to the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals who does not happen to be in the House at the present time. My contention is that in the first place there should be a thoroughly equipped express system between the diifernt provinces and I want to see everything done to facilitate that, but I also want the express companies who have franchises to live up to the conditions that they ask the government to live up to. They ask the government to allow them on the line of the Intercolonial Railway but they will not allow us on their lines. What I would prefer to see if the government is in the railway business is that it should be in the express Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
business as well. Let it own a first-class express system. If it pays a private company to give $100,000 a year for the privilege of operating on the Intercolonial Railway it will pay the government to carry that business on its own account.

Of course, since any litigation has been undertaken under the provisions of this section we have had established a Railway Commission with a supposedly simple method of procedure. The object of this section is very plain. It is undoubtedly to prevent discrimination upon any railway line. I would think that the Railway Commission would be capable of enforcing that section and I do not see any reason why it should not. If the objects of the section are plain and if there is any omission in it which enables that plain object to be defeated, it will be desirable to have such amendment made in the section as to carry out what obviously was the object in the first instance. As far as the Intercolonial Railway is concerned there is a good deal in what my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) suggests:	All that
I brought to the attention of the House the other day was that in the meantime it would be a desirable thing and I should imagine in the interest of the people of the maritime provinces that more than one company should have power to carry on express business on the Intercolonial Railwav. Of course, that power could be given subject to the provision that it should cease at once, should the government decide to establish an express company of its own.

This is a matter that will appertain more particularly to the Department of Railways and Canals but I may say to my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) that I think he will find that there are practical and physical difficulties in the way of operating two or three express companies on the same train. My idea about the fish matter would be that there should be special fish trains. I think that the trade is likely to grow to such proportions as to warrant that and I think, as regards the trade in the United States, that I am correct in saying that special fish trains are run without any reference to the express companies.
Steam service during the season of 1904, between Sydney and Whycocomagh, $1,000.

This is given t* the Bras d'Or Steamship Company, Limited. There has been no alteration in the terminal point. They make two round trips each week.
Steam service during the year 1904, between St. Stephen, N.B., and St. Croix river points, Deer Island, Campobello, and the Inner Islands, Passamaquoddy Bay and L'Etete or Back Bay, $3,000.

This is as usual. The Deer Island and Campobello Steamship Company have the contract and the service is performed by the steamer ' Viking.' They make two round trips each week and they call at a great number of small points.
Steam service during the year 1904, between Quebec and Blanc Sablon, calling at ports and places along the northern shore of the River St. Lawrence between such terminals, $8,0*0.
The contract is with Holliday Brothers and the steamer is the ' King Edward.'
At what ports does this steamer call ? Was this service performed last year ?

Yes, the same service was performed last year. The vessel leaves Quebec and it usually makes no calls till it passes Esquimaux point. Natashquan is the terminal point to be extended as occasion requires to Blanc Sablon. The vessel makes very few calls in the interval.
Is there just one steamer ?

The ' King Edward ' is the only steamer employed. She makes semi-monthly trips.
l^lr. MONK. How many trips were made last year ?

I believe all the trips they were bound to make ; that is to say, semi-monthly trips during the season of navigation were made. There was no interruption, I believe, of the re-' gular trips. What they may have done in the interval I am not aware, but the trips that were called for in the contract were completed.
I do not suppose they made more than eight trips at the most.

My deputy tells me that all the trips from the end of April were made semi-monthly. That would cover about six months, or five and a half months. They stopped only when the buoys were taken up somewhere about the 20th November.
Has the steamer passenger accommodation ?

The ' King Edward ' has. It is a superior steamer and was built expressly for the route.
Steam service during the season of 1904, between Sydney, O.B., and Bay St. Lawrence, calling at way ports, $1,500.

The contract is with the Bras d'Or Steamship Company and the steamer is the ' Weymouth.'
Weekly steamship service between Halifax and Canso, $4,000.
This is done by the steamship ' Strathcona,' owned by the Halifax and Canso Steamship Company.
Is that'the same 'Strathcona ' that is used in the wrecking.

The other I am told is the ' Lord Strathcona ' ; this is plain ' Strathcona.' The wrecking steamer is a very expensive article and we could not possibly hope to get her for $4,000.
Winter steam navigation service during winter of 1904-5, between Quebec and St. Lawrence harbours, down to Murray Bay and River Ouelle, $12,000.
Was anything done last year towards establishing this service?

No, we were not able to get the winter service performed. After a great deal of consideration I understand from my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he has come to the conclusion that it will be necessary to have a special steamer constructed and he proposes to apply to the House for power to have such a steamer put on. The problem of winter navigation of the St. Lawrence, as my hon. friend is aware, is interesting and important, but it is clear that if you are going to make a success you will have to have steamers of un-sual strength and probably of unusual power constructed in order to enable the service to be carried on with any satisfaction, and therefore the minister thinks it will be better to have a steamer built expressly for that service. Later on we will be in a position to give the details about it.

I am glad to hear this announcement because it interests us greatly in Montreal. I think the experiment would be well worth trying because a steamer of that kind would not cost an extremely large amount and even if the experiment proved unsuccessful the steamer would still be of use. My hon. friend will notice that we take power to spend $20,000 a year on steamers going into the Gulf. We have just passed an item of $8,000 for the 1 King Edward ' service.
That is a summer service.
And we have this past two years voted $12,000 for the winter service.
Yes.
We have to guide us the experiments made in Russia under the invention of the late Admiral Makaroff.
You refer to the famous Kronstadt ice-breakers I presume ?

They have been used in the Baltic Sea and on Lake Baikal. I see they

[DOT] 7455

have broken through very thick ice, three, four and five feet or even more. There is no doubt I think that we can also navigate the St. Lawrence, at any rate to Quebec, all through the winter with a steamer of this description. X was surprised in reading a review to observe what a comparatively small amount an ice breaker costs.
Sir RICH Alt D CARTWRIGHT. Does my hon. friend know what such a one as he has referred to costs ?
I do not know the exact figure.
I think the sum is large.

I read several articles in one of the periodical reviews on these Icebreakers. I have not any of the data here but I was surprised at the relatively small cost; it is of course always a considerable sum. I anticipate that a steamer of this description could be used to very good effect in the spring in opening up the navigation to Montreal earlier than the river is naturally opened. There are one or two places in Montreal and Quebec where the bridge is maintained even after the ice is rotten everywhere else. If we -had a steamer of the strength of the ' Ermaak ' for instance, that ice could be easily broken up, and it has been considered by many that the navigation could be opened at least three weeks earlier than at present. That would make an immense difference to the people along the St. Lawrence, between Quebec and Montreal. We spend $20,000 to $25,000 a year on winter navigation from Quebec downwards, and I anticipate that a steamer of that kind would be available in summer as well as in winter. It seems to me it would be easy for us to get a steamer that would be able to obtain the same results as those which are secured in Russia, 'me government could easily obtain exact information as to the cost, &c., of those used in Russia and there is nothing which prevents us following the same course here as has been pursued in that country. I think this should be a matter for the earnest consideration of the government at the earliest possible date. These experiments in Russia date back several years and since reviewers and newspaper men have been able to obtain information pretty exactly it would be easy, I think, for the government to have these results for their guidance. Thus, without spending more than is now being spent very profitable results could be secured.

I dare say that it will prove practicable to do pretty much what my hon. friend has been suggesting. I may say that the subject to which he refers, the extending of the period of navigation from Quebec-and of course if possible from Montreal-by several Mr. MONK.
weeks at the beginning and end of navigation, has attracted the attention both of my own department and of that of Marine, and I understand that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who I regret to say is not present will have certain projects to submit to the House having in view the carrying out of this idea. It is reasonably certain that with proper appliances we could extend the period of navigation from Quebec outward for a considerable period. As to the question of opening it earlier in the spring my hon. friend has stated what is no doubt correct that there are occasional barriers that could be removed by such a steamer, but whether you could depend upon that in view of the enormous masses of ice that are frequently encountered in the gulf to increase the period of navigation in the spring I am not quite so certain.
I refer principally to the inland navigation, so far as the spring is concerned, between Quebec and Montreal.
I was rather referring to ocean navigation. That could undoubtedly be extended. Whether it could be extended all the year is another question.

I agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from Jacques-Car-tier (Mr. Monk). It would undoubtedly be useful and advantageous for the government to have a boat so constructed as to be able to open the ice op the St. Lawrence river above Quebec. I have been living there for upwards of sixteen years, and understand very well how the matter stands. Navigation is sometimes open in Montreal three or four weeks before it is open at Quebec simply because there are no boats at Quebec able to break the ice. Sometimes what is called the key is only about ten miles long in the Narrows at the Quebec bridge and if the government had a boat of the kind described they could open that channel for both local and the general navigation. The steamships from Europe very seldom come to Quebec before the month of May. Of course, they cannot come until the channel is open ; but the government could make preparations to have the channel open from Quebec to Lake St. Peter every year by the 15th of April. Does my hon. friend know what ports it is proposed to stop at from Quebec down to Murray Bay ?

We have not been able as yet to obtain any steamer capable of carrying on that navigation in the winter season, and that fact has led the Minister of Marine to consider the propriety of having a boat built for that express service. When that is obtained it will be at the disposal of the authorities to call at any point that may be thought expedient between Quebec and Murray Bay ;

but I cannot state at what particular points it will call.

There are very few points at which it will be necessary for it to call. The principal point will be Baie St. Paul. On the north shore, from Quebec down to St. Joachim, there will be no need of a steamer, because the cars run there every day ; and on the south shore the country is served by the railway all the way down. Baie St. Paul is well served by a stage route. A steamship mail service on that short route could only be established at a very large expense. Then, in many winters the ice freezes from Quebec down three or four miles, and it would be next to impossible to open a channel through it. I have often heard the ferrymen and the men who handle the boats say that the ice is sometimes fifty, sixty or even one hundred feet thick at Quebec in the winter season.

The points of call for this steamer are I think matters to be decided after the steamer is built and brought here. There are no steamers at present capable of doing the work except those owned by the government of Russia, and therefore a steamer must be built. When the ice is formed I think this steamer will prove to be successful to a certain depth of ice ; but when it comes to the drift ice in the gulf, it will probably have to be discontinued. But I think the experiment is well worth trying in the interest of navigation on the St. Lawrence. *
Summer service between Murray Bay and RiviSre Ouelle, $6,000.
This service was done formerly by the North Transportation Company, and the steamer 4 Admiral ' was employed. It is now conducted by the Intercolonial Railway as a kind of subsidiary service.
Is not the government paying too much for carrying the mail between these two places, especially in the summer time ?

The parties we employed complained bitterly that it was not enough, and withdrew their steamer. We have had a great deal of trouble in getting anything to keep up the navigation there. Of course, a large number of passengers cross between these two points, and the steamer is in a sense a feeder for the Intercolonial.

I think my hon. friend from Dorchester is perhaps right, that this amount is either too much or not enough. The government acted very wisely in establishing this service, which has been very useful, enabling people in Montreal whose families were at Murray Bay to go down on Saturday, and return to their business at Montreal or other western points on Sunday 237J
evening. At the same time, the ' Admiral * is a very old steamer, and the accommodation it provided was most inferior in every way, although a considerable sum, comparatively speaking, was charged for the trip across. For the sum of $6,000 there ought to be a better steamer provided, and the government ought to fix the rate at a more moderate figure. This steamer is a very important feeder for the Intercolonial Railway, and last year it had very large passenger and a considerable freight traffic ; so that its profits must have been considerable. With regard to the larger question of keeping that ferry going all the year round, my hon. friend knows that the ferry between Quebec and L&vis crosses very regularly the whole year round, and it is asserted by many that the crossing between Murray Bay and River Ouelle could be performed just as easily. I think the government ought to consider the advisability of providing such service, either by itself constructing a steamer, or by giving a larger subsidy for a better steamer than that which runs at present. If the opinion which I have obtained is correct, that service could be provided without any very considerable additional expense.
All I can say regarding the subsidy is that the party who got it complained very bitterly that he lost money and would not tender again, and we have had great trouble in supplying the service.

If my memory serves me right, the charge for crossing from Riviere Ouelle to Murray Bay, some eighteen or nineteen miles, is fifty cents, or a dollar for the round trip. In view of the subsidy of $6,000 and the kind of steamer that did the service last year, that seems to be a little excessive. It tends to prevent the extensive traffic that should exist, because that is the only means of daily communication between the north and south ; it would be the sole navigation in winter. This year the government should arrange that the fare shouid be more moderate.

I founl it impossible to get anybody to tender for this service. I tried several times, and sent out several applications. I tried to obtain vessels in the upper lakes since we could not obtain them in Montreal or Quebec, and finally the matter was taken in hand by the Departments of Railways and Marine at my request. At present the Railway Department have borrowed a vessel from the Department of Public Works, and are running it as a kind of ferry. I cannot tell what rates the department are charging, but they have great interest in encouraging the traffic, and am sure will make the charge moderate.

If the department is doing the service, they can control the rates. I strongly call attention to the consideration

that if that service were performed winter and summer and reasonable rates charged, there would be a great traffic indeed over that line, because it is the only outlet th; north shore has. There is no communication between Quebec and Murray Bay except by water. I think that matter should engage the attention of the government.
I have taken a note of what my hon. friend says, and will call the attention of the departments concerned to it. This is quite a recent vote.
Yes, only since two years. It was a very meritorious innovation, and I think could be improved.
What is the name of the boat that is running now ?
It is the ' Eureka,' and belongs to the Public Works Department.

I would ask the right hon. gentleman to look carefully into this matter. I know the boat very well. The department got it when I was minister. An upper deck has been added to it, which causes it to roll very much in a heavy sea. I think, if the hon. minister will look carefully into the case, he will find it advantageous to change this boat for another one soon. I have been on board it many times, and while I would not like to say anything that would injure the line, because I am very favourable to it, I think that the boat has been raised by two decks, and it would be safer to change it for another. I do not want to throw any cold water on the line-very far from it. But I do not think the boat would be able to stand a heavy storm.

The difficulty in getting a boat at all was so serious at one time that it looked as if that service could not be attended to this year. The matter is one of very great importance to the people in that section, especially those on the northern side, and it is a matter of prime importance to the Intercolonial.
Hear, hear.

We have constructed, at considerable expense, the Riviere Ouelle branch for tourist traffic. If a properly constructed and properly kept boat were to run between Rivi&re Ouelle and Murray Bay, the traffic would he very considerable indeed. East year it was quite an important factor in increasing the earnings of the Intercolonial. The matter is having very careful attention, and every activity was displayed during the past two months to procure a boat. There was no other boat available in the Public Works Department, and it was impossible to get one from the Marine Department. There have been negotiations with a view of getting a special boat, and I hope it may be possible, to secure such a Mr. MONK.
boat. I am informed by some parties interested in that section of the country, and particularly by my hon. friend from Charlevoix (Mr. Angers), that this boat is not quite large enough, but she is considered safe and satisfactory for the present. We are putting forth every effort to get a larger boat with a view of later service, and I hav reason to believe that the efforts being put forth by the Marine and Railway Departments, in connection with the Public Works Department, will result in a service being established 'which will accommodate, not merely the summer tourist traffic, but the later traffic of the fall, and even of the winter months.

The boat now in use is a very strong one. I went all around the gulf in it, but that was before the upper decks were added. She draws 12 feet of water. If the captain is a safe man, he will not take the risk of running during a storm, because the boat could not stand a storm, raised as she has been.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Railways anticipate that considerable business will be developed by this line, 'ihe Intercolonial is not paying so much that we would not be glad to see its traffic increase. It would be increased a very great deal if there was really good service there. The boat at present in use is, of course, inadequate for the traffic. I do not know w'ho runs the ferry boats between Quebec and Levis, but the boats are very strong ones, and the owners have no doubt acquired extensive experience in that kind of navigation. If one-half I have heard be true, we could navigate from Murray Bay to Riviere Ouelle almost continuously. The crossing might be interrupted a day or two. but could be carried on pretty regularly. Under these circumstances, I should think my right hon. friend might perhaps call for tenders for the construction of a suitable boat. It would not require a very fine boat, though that might be desirable for summer traffic, but it would require a good, strong, safe boat; and, the traffic being what I anticipate between the north and south shore and over the Intercolonial, it would require a boat of considerable size. I think the matter ought to be attended to without delay.
Steam communication between Prince Edward Island, Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $8,000.
This was a contract with Messrs. Hugh McMillan and Henry Aitken.

What will be the starting point in the province of Prince Edward Island for this service and what will be the port or ports of call in that province ? Also, what will be the port or ports of call in Cape Breton and the port of destination in Newfoundland ?
Leaving Charlottetown, thence to Bridgetown, An-nandale and Souris, Prince Edward Island ; thence to Glace Bay and Sydney, and thence to St. John's, Newfoundland ; returning over the same route.
In any agreement that may be made with a company for this service, that will be one of the conditions, of course ?

That is our intention, of course.
Steam service between Canada and Australia, $194,666.66.
What steamers perform this service ? What is the frequency of the trips ; and what trade, if any, has been developed ; also between what ports in Canada and Australia is the service conducted ?
The service is performed by the steamships ' Mio-wera,' ' Aorangi,' and ' Moana.' It is a foui-weekly service, and is carried on from Vancouver to Sydney.
Is this the same as the service to Japan ?
This is in the nature of an experiment to see if we can prolong that service during the winter months. We are now in negotiation and hope to obtain the service.
We had an item in the estimates for this year ; did the hon. minister utilize that ?

For the service of a wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence for the year ending June 30, 1905, $10,000.
This is in the nature of a retainer. For this the wrecking plant must be held in readiness constantly to go to any vessel that may be in trouble.
When did the government begin granting this subsidy ?
I think it was two years ago.

As the hon. minister is aware this same firm has been in the wrecking business for the last thirty years. The same plant has always been kept in readiness. These people have been making a lot of money annually. About two years ago when Captain Leslie, of Kingston, whom the hon. minister knows well, removed his wrecking plant down to that district to take part in assisting these vessels that were wrecked, and spent an immense amount of money, the hon. minister immediately gave this other wrecking firm a subsidy. By this, of course, Captain Leslie is placed at a disadvantage. It seems most unfair that when a gentleman with the ability of Captain Leslie, a gentleman whom, I am sure, the minister will say is a most reliable man and whose wrecking plant is a very tine one, removes clown there, he should be met with a subsidy to an opposition concern. This wrecking firm has been in existence for thirty or forty years without a subsidy, and I would like to know wThy this subsidy of $10,000 is now paid to it within the last two of three years. What is the necessity for it? They had their plant there, I saw the plant there ten years ago, they had an enormous plant of their own. They have some vessels, I think they sold the ' Lord Stanley,' but they have got the ' Strathcona,' a vessel of about the same size. There seems to be something wrong in this matter when a subsidy is given at this particular time, though another wrecking outfit has, gone down there.

So far as I remember, the subsidy was granted to the Messrs. Davis before Captain Leslie had gone down there at all. I think it is only within the last year or two that Captain Leslie has gone dow-n the St. Lawrence.
He has been there some time.

In the next place, the ' Lord Strathcona ' is a very much more powerful boat and has much better appliances for wrecking than any that have been in the service before. I can only say that this was a request upon the government *by, I think, the entire shipping interests in the St. Lawrence. An enormously large and influential petition was presented to us, and I remember' that a large deputation called on myself and I think the Premier. The whole of the shipping interests of the St. Lawrence made a request to us that we would see that this service was kept constantly in the best condition. Unless this grant was given it would be optional with Mr. Davis to have taken his craft anywhere, and I believe he had beeu in the habit of taking it occasionally far

outside the St. Lawrence to assist vessels in distress to go to Boston and New York. I have no wish, as the hon. gentleman knows himself, to discriminate in favour of one against the other ; but when the whole St. Lawrence trade come to us and request that we should insist on this vessel being kept steadily in readiness, it seems to me a proper request to make, and everybody knows that at that time the St. Lawrence route was a little in disfavour owing to the number of accidents that happened and the great difficulty in bringing assistance to vessels in distress. Since this grant has been made a very considerable salvage of property has been successfully effected, which, I think, could not have been affected unless this vessel had been always in hand and ready to go out.

I know that Capt. Leslie has effected quite a lot of salvage since he has been down there, and I know for a fact that his wrecking plant is just the same now as it has been for the last ten or twelve years.

The ' Lord Strathcona ' is a much better vessel than they ever had before.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. I think the 'Lord Stanley ' was the best steamer there previously. I have seen the ' Lord Stanley ' and she was the larger vessel. They have purchased the ' Strathcona ' since this subsidy was given and they are making a large amount of money there yearly. They never went to Boston, because there is a large wrecking plant at Boston which they could not interfere with. It is a very easy matter for Mr. Davis to get up a petition and every one of the vessel men will sign it ; they would not want to refuse for fear they might get into trouble themselves. As this wrecking firm has been in existence for the last thirty or forty years, and in addition the government have given them the Levis dry dock,-
I am not aware of that.

I understand that to be the case. This has all been given free, and if such is the case, it does seem strange that the government should now give this subsidy. In addition, by giving this subsidy, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is doing his best to get Captain Leslie and his fleet off the St. Lawrence. I know for a fact that he has saved vessels when the ' Strathcona ' could not get there soon enough. I think it would be fair for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to divide this subsidy with Mr. Leslie, or else give him a subsidy as -well, because he has rendered great services to the shipping industry. I think the minister should be a little easier with Captain Leslie and not give these people a subsidy that will have the effect Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
of driving him out of business and thus leave the vessel men in that locality at the mercy of one firm.
Sir RICHARD CARTW'RIGHT. This objection will apply, I am afraid, to a great many subsidies besides the present one. But I am advised that the 1 Lord Strathcona ' is very much the most powerful steamer that has ever been engaged in the wrecking business on the St. Lawrence. The first subsidy was granted to an inferior steamer, the one the hon. gentleman referred to, the ' Stanley.'
When was that granted?

A matter of three or four years ago.

Steamboat service between Canada and Mexico, $50,000.

With respect to this vote I may say to the committee that contracts have been called for the purpose of ascertaining whether we can promote communication between Canada and Mexico. The Mexican government have agreed to give a similar sum of $50,000. We will receive in a little while, I hope, some communication on this head. The intention is, in the first place, to see if we can establish a service on the Pacific coast from Vancouver and Victoria, touching at various points on the Mexican Pacific ocean. If we .succeed in that we will also see if we can establish a service on the other side, going from points in the Gulf of Mexico up to St. ,Tohn and Halifax. As yet we are not in a position to say how far our negotiations will be successful, or what tenders we will receive. I trust in a short time that I shall be in receipt of the information.
Were tenders issued in the first instance calling for a service on the Pacific side ?

They called for both. But the Mexican government appeared to think that it would be better for them to have a service on the Pacific side, and they propose to devote the major part of their subsidy to that side. We are at a disadvantage no doubt in the Gulf of Mexico owing to the number of American routes that converge there. I should like myself to see the service established on both sides of the continent, but we may have to confine ourselves in the first instance to the western side. If the hon. gentleman remembers the geographical configuration of Mexico, he will see that our

chances are better on the Pacific coast than on the Atlantic coast at present.
What is the nature of the trade that is expected to be done ?
What is the amount of our export and import trade ?

Our trade with Mexico is very small at the present time but it is probable that a certain amount of our exports go to Mexico via New York and are classified as imports from the United States. The total amount of trade is very small at the present time. Whether we can develop a larger trade remains to be seen.
This is somewhat in the nature of an experiment ?

This is in the nature of an experiment but we have thought that when the Mexican government have displayed so much good-will we might better meet them. There are good reasons why we and the Mexicans stand particularly well with each other.

Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

This pier was completed for a length of about 175 feet. It requires about 125 feet of further extension and it is estimated that the cost will be [DOT]51,500. The same remarks apply to the next item for $1,500 for the pier at Burleigh.

We require to deepen the channel between Lakefield and Young's point in a number of places as during periods of low water the boats ground.

Because it is an old part of the canal that has been navigable.
We generally have to make a complaint the other way.
I know, we are damned if we do and damned if we don't.

I am not going to object to this.
Trent canal-blasting and dredging channel above lock 1, Lakefield, $3,000.

The water here is very shallow and requires to be deepened at least two feet. This work is all done by contract except the dredging. We have a dredge and do our own dredging.
Trent canal-to provide one dredging engine! boiler and steel boom, $6,500.
Is that awarded by tender and contract ?

We will ask for tenders. There was an item last year for the rebuilding of the hull of the dredge ' Otona-bee.' That has been completed and it was intended to place the machinery of the old dredge in the new hull but it was found that the amount of repairs on the machinery would be so great that it is deemed more economical to purchase new machinery. We will ask for tenders from the trade.
Do you simply write to a few firms in the trade ?
We advertise in the newspapers.
Is that going to be the rule ? It has not been done for the last few years.
I have been doing it right along.
You have not been there very long.
There is an improvement already.
Is this to be advertised ?
I assume that no change will take place ; I have not contemplated any change.
There were a great many cases along the canals where tenders were not called for in the newspapers.

That is only in the case where there are only a few manufacturers of certain articles in which case we send a circular to them and so avoid the expense of advertising, but with respect to cement and all other items of that kind in connection with the canal, so far as I have had any experience in the department and been able to observe, general advertisements are placed in the newspapers. I know that every newspaper in the country wants an advertisement.
Prior to 1896 the government would advertise for tenders along the St. Lawrence in the local papers.
So we do now.
Tell me of one newspaper along the St. Lawrence canal in which there is given an advertisement for supplies ?

I do not suppose my hon. friend reads some of the newspapers in which the advertisements are to be found or he would see them. We cannot advertise in all the papers. I know that we advertise in the Peterborough, Hamilton, Toronto and Ottawa papers. We are sometimes a little select; we have to select one out of a great number.	[DOT]

No tenders are called for locally by advertisement but letters are sent to a few friends of the government asking them what they will furnish supplies for, and the same thing applies to the building of scows.

I say most distinctly with reference to the scows that we would not invite general competition all over the province. That would cost more for advertising than the amount appropriated. In the immediate vicinity there will be a general advertisement. There are three dump scows required in that section of the country for which we ask $2,500 in this vote and the public will have an opportunity of competing, but it would be unwise and unbusinesslike to ask for tenders all over the province owing to the expense of advertising.
Mr. 'J. D. REID. I would like to know why tenders are not asked for along the St. Lawrence for supplies or for the building of scows. If the minister would advertise in one or two papers, one in each county along the St. Lawrence, I am sure that would not be asking too much. There are dozens of men there who can furnish sup-Mr. A. T. THOMPSON.
plies or build any scows required. The cost of the supplies for the maintenance of the canals has been almost doubled since 1896, and I do not believe one tender has been called for in the last seven years. The parties furnishing these supplies are outside of the county, and there are many people in the county friends of the government too, who would be glad to furnish these supplies. Therefore I think the government should adopt the system of advertising for tenders instead of distributing these orders without proper competition. It is understood that these shall be advertised for tender ?
Yes.

In connection with the dredging along the Trent waterway.
Trent canal-to complete rebuilding dam at Peterborough, $4,000.

In the main estimates. I do not see my hon. friend from East Durham (Mr. Ward) here. He wants to speak on the subject, and I am going to arrange so that he will have the opportunity to do so.

I do not know.

proximately 60 cents a yard, as a dredge *will liave to be brought from a distance for a few day's work. The whole is expected to cost about $2,000.
Rideau canal-to rebuild bridge at Smith's Falls, $5,000.

This is to rebuild a bridge across the west channel of the Rideau canal, below the basin, at the town of Smith's Falls. The present bridge was built many years ago of timber, and lias been repaired and maintained ever since. It is over twenty years old, and is beyond repair.
Has the minister made any arrangement for /rebuilding the dam at Poonamalee ?

That will necessarily be provided later on. we could not in the main estimates, which were prepared before the accident occurred.
presents an interest charge on $75,000 at the rate the government pays interest.

An attempt was made to do away with it. One-third of the dam was blown up but the lumbermen universally protested. They said that even though abolished as a canal and even though the government repudiated liability in connection with it, yet it should remain as it was, so that they might get whatever benefit from it they could.
