Chambly canal-to macadamize towpath,
This is to macadamize ten and half miles nine feet wide, twelve inches deep in centre and nine inches at the sides. It will .be let by tender and contract.
Has any of the towpath been macadamized heretofore ?

I hope some provision will be made for covering the damages caused by the breaking of the dam.
Culbute canal-damages by flooding caused by dams of the canal, $2,305.
Is this an annual charge ? What does it mean ?

Yes, this towpath was a number of years metallized with gravel from Lake Champlain. It is now almost impossible to procure this material, and as the metal is practically worn out, we must substitute macadam, ordinary macadam without delay. It is supposed to cost $3,000 per mile. The amount asked for will only macadamize three miles.

This canal is on the Ottawa river. The canal has not been much used, and very serious damage has been caused by flooding. For 1903-4 there was an appropriation of $2,315, which was paid. The damages were inquired into by Mr. Surtees, civil engineer, of Ottawa.
Is not that kept in regular repair annually ? Last year quite an amount was spent.
That was in connection with the road and not the towpath.
Is not the towpath kept

If it is a case of permanent flooding, one would have supposed that the land covered by the waters thrown back by the dam should be expro-jiriated once for all. If that is not the case, I would like to understand just what the situation is. It seems unusual that a charge for flooding should be an annual charge.

This canal is now abandoned entirely and by proclamation has been done away with. That was done within the last two or three months. It was built previous to confederation for the benefit of the lumbermen on the Ottawa river. There was only sufficient land procured for the purposes of the canal and none purchased to guard against flooding, and the result has been damages from year to year. An unusual damage occurred a year ago last spring near the township of Allumette Island and under the advice of the Justice Department we made the best settlement we could.
One would suppose that if the canal were no longer useful, it would be better to do away with the dam instead of paying $2,500 annually, which rein repair regularly ?

Yes. The towpath is on one side of the canal and the road on the other. Some portions of the roadway were macadamized last year, and a vote was given a few years ago to macadamize a further portion of the road.
Surely $3,000 a mile is a very large amount to macadamize a narrow road.

I can give the estimate. The cost per mile for the material, labour and rolling is $3,025. That is the amount made up toy the engineer. Of course we will ask for public tender and will then discover whether this is too high an estimate or not.

What position can the government take in so far as the collection of tolls is concerned ? There are $34,008 paid for the collection of canal tolls and none have been collected for the last two years. There is no reason why the lock-masters should not be utilized to issue passes and thus save $34,000 per annum. Even though there were a mistake in the lockmaster issuing passes, it is easily recti-

lied. It seems to me that that amount of $'14,008 should be saved.
. Mr. EMMERSON. As my hon. friend knows, it was determined to try the experiment of abolishing the tolls on the canals for two years and see what effect that would have on the traffic of the country. It was also stated that these men, some of whom were long in the service, should be continued in order to keep an accurate record of the business done. After this year, the whole matter will be determined. It_may be that the tolls will be permanently abolished, but we will know from the returns given just what the effect has been.
This is the second year. What was the result of the year's operations ? Did it increase trade ? Are the results such that the government would continue the present free system ?

Last year there was some improvement. As to this year, judging by what has been done up to this date, it would be a question whether, taking the average into consideration, there has been an improvement in the trade.

I do not think that the re-imposition of the tolls would be a good move. The abandonment of the tolls tends to bring more trade by the St. Lawrence route. But, for the very reason that I think the tolls should not be re-imposed, I feel very strongly that the government should at once reduce that expense. If the hon. minister will not do it this year, I hope that next year the government-whatever government may be in power-will put it right.

Any opinion offered by my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid), or by myself, on that subject, could be only a casual opinion, and the government could not act upon it. It is necessary to have accurate information with respect to the trade. On the basis of that accurate information the government will determine what is the best policy. I know how difficult it would be to restore the tolls, even though in the judgment of the country it would be wise to do so.

The lockmasters are quite capable of issuing the passes which would be the basis of the information. OI course, where money had to be collected- and it was collected in large amounts-the lockmasters, perhaps, did not wish to take the responsibility of holding that monev. especially for the small salaries they a>-e getting. But there is no reason they should not issue the passes. It does seem ridiculous and absurd that a man should be paid $1,000 for doing work that the lockmaster, who is already under pay, could do. And this work is done by the lockmasters on the Rideau canal. That being so, why cannot the lockmasters do it on the St. Lawrence canal ?

It would not do to do this work in a careless or haphazard way. This information was necessary. Quite a number of these men were in the service, and, to carry out the hon. gentleman's idea, they would have to be superannuated or dismissed ; with the result, possibly, that at the end of two or three years it would be necessary to fill their places again. The extra expense is certainly not to be taken into consideration as against the importance of the information that [DOT] these gentlemen are required to secure and furnish for the department.
The minister's statement is a reflection upon the men on the Rideau canal, who actually do this work.

Nobody has been dismissed on the Rideau canal. The men who were doing this work before on the Rideau canal are doing it now just as on the other canals.
Canals, miscellaneous-surveys and inspections, $3,000.
This is an ordinary annual vote. The expenditure under this head for the year ending 30th June, 1904, was $3,252.18.

Since, the death of the late Mr. Rubidge, the steamer ' Alert ' has been in charge of the superintendent of canals in that district. Surely the government are not going to furnish the superintendent with a pleasure yacht to run up and down the canal. There has never been anything of that kind in the history of this country on any of the canals. This boat, in fact, is larger than the ordinary pleasure yacht; she is a steamer that costs $8,000 or $10,000 per annum to run.

The steamer 'Alert' has been for years employed on the canals that were under the supervision of the superintending engineer, Mr. Rubidge. By the death of Mr. Rubidge the office became vacant, and it has not been filled. In the meantime the boat has been placed in charge of the superintendent of canals in the same way as the rest of the plant connected with the canals. At one time, in addition to the superintending engineer, they had a superintendent of the Cornwall canal and also a superintendent of the Williamsburgh canal. The present superintendent. Mr. Stewart, is now in charge of both canals. He has to go from one place to the other. The point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) is one that occurred to my own mind as to the necessity of continuing the steamer. If the dredging is to be done and the engineers- even though there is no superintending engineer-have to get out at the different points, and if the superintendent has to go to the different canals, it may be necessary, for the present at least, to continue the steamer. Meantime, I purpose taking into consideration whether some cheaper method

cannot be devised, and tins steamer placed elsewhere or disposed of.

I remember the way the * Alert ' first came on that route. A number of years ago the government had under construction the Cornwall canal, the Farran's Point canal, the Williamsburgh canal, the North Channel and the Galops Rapids. At each one of these works there was an engineer in charge. The late Mr. Rubidge was superintending engineer over all me works, and the government furnished him with this ste&mer to enable him to run up and down and inspect them. These works have practically all been completed, and there is nothing going on at the present time except at Galops Rapids and the North Channel, which are side by side. At that time there were two superintendents not very distant from each other. When a change of government took place it was decided to abolish their positions, and these two men were dismissed, and Mr. Rubidge was placed in charge of all the canals as well as of the work of construction. These two men that were dismissed were Dr. Hickey and Mit Ross. Shortly after it was decided that it would be well to appoint two men as assistants, but practically they were in the same position as the others had been. One is Mr. Tally at Cornwall, just as able a man as Dr. Hickey or Mr. Ross. One was appointed for Morrisburg and one for Cornwall, with Mr. Stewart superintending the two systems. Now we have got the same number of men as before, though they are called by different names. Mr. Stewart is over the canal in the same way that Mr. Rubidge was, except that he has no construction work to do. I am satisfied that this expenditure of $8,000 or $10,000 per annum for this steamer running up and down, is waste of money. Suppose this man wants to go from Morrisburg to Cornwall, a distance of twelve or thirteen miles. In the olden times the superintendent hired a livery man to drive him up at a cost of $2 or $3 per day, while the cost in the whole season would probably be $300 or $400. But now this steamer is put on, with a crew, and it will cost a lot to run her up and down. A pleasure party will be brought on board of this steamer, and she will run up to Cornwall and on as far as Prescott, and then turn and head down towards Williamsburg probably at a cost of $50- for the trip ; whereas the superintendent could drive along the whole system in a couple of hours and at very small expense. Now the government have put on a boat which is a laughing stock for the whole public, even strong Liberals cannot believe that it will be continued. It is such an outrageous thing that the government should drop it. I was told the other day that Mr. Stewart had started out with a great pleasure picnic from
Morrisburg, simply going to Cornwall, I presume.

I don't know as to that. I am satisfied that Mr. Stewart will not make any improper use of the boat, or anv use that is not necessary in connection with the canal. My hon. friend knows that Mr. Rubidge had this steamer for all these years, and I do not know that my hon. friend made any serious complaint about the cost.
I complained about this steamer every year, about its being kept up for Mr. Rubidge's service after the work was completed.

Mr. Rubidge only died a month ago, and the matter came under my observation very recently. I have not had an opportunity of looking into it myself. I hoped the session would have been through before now, and that I would have an opportunity of going down there and studying the situation. In the meantime this boat has been placed under the charge of the superintendent of these canals, who is the proper man to have charge of her. Also there are some engineers engaged finishing up the work, and this boat is placed at their disposal the same as Mr. Rubidge used it in connection with the canal works. I shall determine what to do, and if we find that the work of the superintendent can be carried on by the use of a train or in any other way, the cheapest and best course will be adopted.
I understand that when Mr. Rubidge died Mr. Rheaume was placed in charge.

Mr. Stewart is simply using the boat to run up and down the canal. Mr. Rubidge had not done much with the boat during the present season because he was too ill, and the boat was lying at Cornwall doing nothing. I do not know why it should be taken out and put on a new service running up and down the canal. It it bad been placed in Mr. Stewart's charge to be responsible for it, that would be a different thing. Every time she goes out it means a lot of money. Mr. Stewart goes down to Cornwall armed with a letter from the department, showing that this boat is handed over to him. is in his charge and that he can do as he likes with it because it is handed over to the engineering staff,

and Mr. Rheaume's responsibility for it has been taken away.

Mr. Itheaume was ill no way responsible for that boat. Mr. Stewart, the superintendent of the eanal is responsible for its proper use just in the same way as he is responsible for any other plant in connection with the canal. He is instructed to place the boat at the disposal of the engineers in connection with the work on the canal. He is now using it in connection with the work on the canal.

He is employing it for his own use on the canal. There is no work of any kind going on now. I hope that when this matter comes up again it will be straightened out in such a way that the public as a whole can feel that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals does not wish to put an expenditure upon these canals such as was never known or that no person, either Liberal or Conservative, would undertake to justify.
I would like to know why the vote is required. Is not this inspection and survey made by officers of the department V And if so, what is the purpose of the vote V
Are you referring to the $3,000 ?
Yes.

This is in connection with the travelling expenses of officers. Officers of the department and resident engineers are sent out to different points from time to time and this is to cover their expenses.
How much did you expend last year V
Mr. LfeNNOX. You are asking for $3,000 and this is a revote.

It is an annual vote, not a revote.
Railways and canals-surveys and inspections, railways, $18,000.
This is for the same thing.

If the hon. minister will refer to the Auditor General's Report for 1903, pages W-48 and W-47, he will find an account of the expenses of the cattle-guard commission amounting to $6,942.83. Then it says :
Less charged to surveys and inspections, railways (page W-47), $1,946.61.
leaving an apparent total of $4,996.22. I want to know from the hon. minister what is the reason for taking off that $1,946.61 ? That is a portion of the expenses incurred in con-Mr. J. D. REID.
neetion with the railway cattle-guard commission. Turning back to page W-47 we find, referring to that item of $1,946.61, the expenses of Mr. F. W. Holt, under the heading of ' Miscellaneous surveys and inspections ; cattle-guard commission ' showing that this is an item in connection with the cattle-guard commission and that alone. I refer to that because of the somewhat peculiar system of bookkeeping which seems to obtain and for the purpose of calling attention to the fact that the commission actually cost us $6,492.83. In collection with the matter I had occasion to ask some questions a short time ago. The questions and answers appear in ' Herald ' of the 13th July last. I asked :
Did the services of Geo. Robertson, Esq., as commissioner, from August 16, 1902, to February 13, 1903, 181 days, include a Sunday service as such commissioner ?
The hon. Minister of Public Works gave the following answer to that question :
Mr. Robertson was paid $5 per day for days he actually worked, which did not include Sundays, and reasonable travelling expenses and living expenses when absent from home.
As a matter of fact the hon. minister will find, whether it is due to an error or otherwise, that, if he takes the dates that Mr. Robertson puts in his own account

Services : Aug. 16, 1902-Feb. 13, 1903, 181 d. at $5, $905.
-it includes every Sunday. It surely could not have been the intention that Mr. Robertson should work on behalf of the country in connection with the inspection of cattle-guards and superintending the general conduct of that wall-eyed steer on Sundays as well as on other days of the week. I do not know how it is that the hon. minister gives the answer in the way he does saying that he was only paid for the actual work he did not including Sundays.
I got the answer from the accountant of the department.
It is not a matter of great importance but it is as well to be correct.
Certainly, I supposed the accountant to be correct.

If the hon. minister will add up the figures he will find that they include every day. I also find from the returns that have been brought down that there is a difficulty between Mr. F. W. Holt, one of the commissioners and the government. I have asked whether the difficulty has been adjusted but I have not received an answer. Probably the hon. minister will answer me and say whether the matter is settled or not.
I can tell the hon. gentleman how the matter stands.

Probably I had better say what I have to say. While Mr. Holt got for his services $150 a month he is claiming a thousand dollars more, according to his correspondence. He gives reasons which I think ought to commend themselves to the minister although I do not know whether they would commend themselves to the farming community. I notice in connection with these accounts that the grievances which used to be urged against the Conservative Premier in regard to the charging of cab-hire are continued by the Liberal government. There are also charges here for the polishing of these gentlemen's boots which I suppose would have to be done if they were at home. They also include an account for the expenses of providing office room at St. John and so on. I find that Mr. Holt says that the arrangement made with him by the government was that he should get $150 a month and his actual expenses. He claims that he is entitled to more money. These expenses include not only items such as I have mentioned but they also include railway fare. If the railways are to be exonerated from the payment of any other sum I think they might at least have been asked to bear that part of the expense, to carry these parties from place to place. Mr. Holt further claims that he is entitled to extra compensation and in writing to Mr. Schreiber on the 7th of January, 1904, he puts in this very weightly claim. I want to call the attention of the minister to it, and indirectly the attention of the country, as indicating exactly what was done on behalf of the people in the matter of cattle-guards and the kind of investigation that actually took place in this matter. Mr. Holt says :
When the tests were completed we had not then found a thoroughly satisfactory guard	 It then became my duty to find out the reason

I have some doubt about that, but that is what he says :
.-the only way to do this was to study the structure of the animal as a piece of mechanism. This has been done as to his anatomy by the veterinarian as a surgeon, but I have been unable to find an idea as to his capacity as a machine other than in his ordinary walk.
I suppose he menus his ordinary walk in life.
In emergency motions as in passing a cattle-guard.
It breaks off abruptly there. I do not know exactly what he means. I suppose he means that no special study has been made of the animal in emergency motions as in passing a cattle guard.
And it was from this point of view I have had to treat it. In making this search, I have found that there is very little literature available to the general reader, &e.
And upon this basis he contends that he is to apply himself seriously to this matter, studying this question seriously from the standpoint of the mechanism of the animal and his action in cases of emergency and that he is therefore entitled to at least $1,000 more. I do not know how the government looks upon it, but he gives very good reasons, and I am sorry to say casts some doubt upon the bona fides of the government in this matter. He says :	I went
at it seriously, I thought the government were in earnest. He does not say that the government were not in earnest but he suggests that the government did not bona fide intend to find out a suitable and sufficient cattle-guard. I would be glad to have an explanation from the minister as to the position in which the account stands, as it does not appear to be closed.
Mr. EMMER'SON. It seems to be generally admitted by Mr. Holt and all interested that he was employed in connection with this commission at a fixed rate of payment which was settled at the rate of $150 per month and all his actual travelling expenses and other expenses incident to the work of himself and his co-commissioner. He was paid in accordance with that agreement but subsequently he presented to the department a claim for an additional amount because he had been employed longer than he had anticipated when he accepted the position. Mr. Holt, is, I may say, an engineer of good reputation, and personally I would speak in the highest terms of him both as a man and, so far as I had experience with him, as an engineer. He was arbitrator with Mr. Walter Shanley and Mr. Surtees in a celebrated case in New Brunswick in connection with which I was employed as one of the counsel. Later on I appeared before a tribunal of which he was a member and I may say that on both of these occasions he distinguished himself by the care with which he considered everything and the attention he gave to the cases and the arguments presented before the court. As I knew him well professionally and personally as a friend, he, naturally, after I came into office, presented his view of the case to me. Although the matter had been determined by the department previous to my accession to office he thought I would review it. I did so ; I went into the matter very closely, and I felt that an agreement having been made and carried out both by himself and the department I could not recommend that the decision of the department should either be reviewed or set aside by action of the Council. I felt tkat the Auditor General too would not authorize any departure from an agreement which had been carefully entered into and acted upon by both parties to it. Under these circumstances, while I would have liked very much to have seen him get an additional amount I felt that by reason of the agreement entered into by

7480'
him it was impossible to allow him any additional compensation, even although the time occupied by him was longer than he had anticipated. Usually in such cases when men are willing to work for so much a month the more months the merrier, and I would rather argue it from that standpoint, but in this case a different view was taken by Mr. Holt. I am sorry that Mr. Holt was dissatisfied with the decision but I certainly could not reverse it and I think that the judgment of this committee will be that the decision arrived at by me was correct.

Does the minister think that Mr. Holt was required to spend as much time as he claims to have spent in this investigation ? Has the minister satisfied himself as to the length of time he took in making this supposed investigation ? I ask this because the prevailing opinion in Ontario, so far as I can understand, is that ten times as much time was consumed as was necessary and not one-tenth as much information was obtained as should have been secured. Any ordinary man, not claiming to be (especially skilful can find cattle-guards that will turn cattle at a crossing. This gentleman seems to have spent month after month in accomplishing nothing, whether he was trying to accomplish anything or not I do not know but his effort seemed to be to find some defect in every cattle-guard which was submitted for his examination. I attended almost every meeting of that commission in Ontario and I know that a great deal of useful information was submitted to him and many models were shown to him but he did not find any of these worthy of consideration. He seems to have gone off to discover the structure of the animal and how he would walk in an emergency. I cannot understand for the life of me what Mr. Holt was getting at there unless he was trying to make a report to this government that the railways could not get an effective cattle-guard.
I repeat that at all the meetings in Ontario at which I was present, and I was at all but two, a great many good structures were offered to these gentlemen ; and there were no two opinions that many of them were effective, and would turn back ninety-nine out of one hundred animals. Tne hon. gentleman, not expecting at that time to be Minister of Railways, probablj did not go down to the fair grounds here, as I did, when Mr. Holt was experimenting, or he' would have found that the situation which Mr. Holt was trying to deal with there was not the situation as it existed in the country at all. He did not have a highway, from which the anfmai would have to turn aside to the right or the left to get on the railway, but he constructed a railway, and put the animal on the track, and surrounded the track with human beings on both sides, and urged the animal along the track and over the guard to the open highway; and as the

animal had no other way to go, he struggled across. Therefore, because the animal got over the guard, Mr. Holt said the guard would not turn back the animal. That was very different from the situation in the country which Mr. Holt was employed to investigate. Therefore I think Mr. Holt has been very well paid, particularly as he chose to make a bargain at $5 a day ; but I wonder that the minister did not tell him that three-fourths of his time was wasted, and that the commission accomplished nothing. X do not know why the report of this commission has not been published and circulated through the country. X can only suppose that it is because it does not contain the information which the government thought it ought to contain. Perhaps it is not a work of very great literary quality; but I do know that when this matter was brought up in the House, the reason the late Minister of Railways gave for not making the railways liable was that he was going to have the matter investigated by a commission, and that when he found what was the safest and ,most effective guard-a guard which he might call the standard-he would pass a law to make the railways adopt it; and they would be liable if they did not adopt it and not liable if they did and it failed to turn iback the cattle. But, like many things which this government has promised, that did not happen, and we got the law which was contended for by myself and others on this side of the House, making the railways liable in any event and allowing them to provide their own guard. We are now dealing with the cost of this commission. I understand that Mr. Holt got $5,000, and that he wants $100 a month more. I think the minister, when inquiring into this question, ought to see whether or not Mr. Holt earned the money he did get. The farmers of the country, who are paying this expenditure of $6,000, which they have always claimed through their representatives in this House who knew anything about the matter, was a useless expenditure, believe that the results of this commission have been absolutely nil to the country. I think the Minister of Railways owes it to the farmers who pay the larger portion of the taxes of this country, to see whether Mr. Holt earned the money he did get or not, and, if he did not, to have it refunded. The farmers do not know what particular instructions were given to Mr. Holt; but they have a right to suppose that he was instructed to do his best to ascertain what is the best guard that could be obtained. I understand that the report says that there is no guard that can be obtained that will turn cattle. Now, the farmers of this country will not swallow that; I may as well tell the minister that first as last, I may also tell him that at these cattle-guard meetings il saw models of a good many guards with which the commissioners could not find fault; but they did try to find fault with every guard presented to them.

Several questions were discussed at these meetings as to the structure of the guards ; opinions were taken from the farmers and mechanics present as to what sort of mechanical contrivance should be used ; and I have looked in vain in the commissioner's report for all that evidence. If it is so as I gather from the hon. member for South Simcoe, that these gentlemen, charged railway fares while travelling through Ontario, that is an imposition on the country, because I was on the train with them, and I know they travelled from one place to another on passes which were furnished to them by the railways. I know they did not pay their railway fares then.
My hon. friend does not say that they charged for railway expenses which they did not pay out 1
I do not think they have charged all their railway fares, but they have charged some.
That is, where they had not passes.

I might ask the hon. minister if it is the intention of the goveimment to publish the report of this commission ? It should be published unless that involves a large expense, because we might as well know what was done. It looks to me as if it could be published at an expense of a very few dollars, judging by the public accounts, where there is a charge for a typewritten report of the commission, COO copies, at 5 cents each, $30. If it is a 5 cent report, I think we ought to have copies of it.
Is not that 5 cents per folio ?
I do not see anything to show that it is 600 folios.

I have been asked by my hon. friend from Lincoln as to whether I thought Mr. Holt took up more time than was necessary. If I were to answer that question, I would say that if more time was taken than was actually necessary, it was not done intentionally or for any improper purpose by Mr. Holt. I have a sufficiently high opinion of him to reach that conclusion. There is a great difference between men in this respect. Some are quick in thought, in action and in speech. Some are slow in thought and in speech. Mr. Holt may have been slow in his methods to work out the ideas he had before him, but he claimed to me it was necessary for him to take thal time, and that he was entitled to some additional compensation.
Because he was slow ?

No ; he claimed that he did the work with great rapidity, and that the speed made by him in reaching a conclusion was a further reason why he should
be paid more. I have decided against Mr. Holt, although he is a personal and, I believe, a political friend of my own. I am informed that Mr. Holt did not urge the cattle in any direction on this track. The Deputy Minister of Railways was there, and he said that the only thing that was done was to place hay on the track on either side of the cattle-guard, and the cattle were driven, along and, seeing the hay, they turned in its direction. I intend studying the report, which I have not yet had time to do, but as the matter comes under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, I have felt that it was incumbent upon that commission rather than me to deal with it.

In view of what the minister has said, I can only say that there must be a double sort of structure down at the grounds where these experiments were made, because I not only saw the animals forced over the guards, but remonstrated with Mr. Holt about the way they were treated. His answer was that he wanted to put each guard to the strictest possible test. I toid him two or three times that it was not a fair test to force an animal over the guard. Thfere was no way for the animal to escape except to struggle over the guard. As regards the printing and publishing of this report, the only reason I can see for publishing it would be to show the farmers what little value this government gives them for their money.

I am in favour of the government publishing the report. As I understand from the hon. minister, the cost will not be very great. The government has already expended about $5,000 in testing cattle-guards
Almost $7,000.
I stand corrected. As the government has spent almost $7,000 in testing cattle-guards
No. I do not understand my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) to say we have expended $7,000 in testing cattle-guards.	[DOT]
The country has been expending $7,000 for the purpose of testing cattle-guards to find
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) has a right to choose his own language. I only wanted to know what he meant.
I only wished to state the case as it is. So, I will ask the hon. minister to explain it to me.

of the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals-another illustration that if half a dozen men attend a dog fight each will give a different account of it. I do not know that the hon. minister has made it much clearer. I made the statement that the cost of testing the cattle-guards was about $7,000, and I understand that the exact figure is $0,942. This money has been spent in the effort to find out whether a suitable cattle-guard had been invented. I think that some of the guards submitted for examination were very suitable and might be adopted by the railways in Canada. I know of one, patented by a gentleman from Cookville, Ont., and brought to the city at considerable cost to the inventor, to be submitted to tests. X understand that for more than an hour and a half in one case, and more than two hours in the other case, the cattle were unable to get over this cattle-guard. The inventor felt that it would be a suitable cattle-guard for use on our railways, and if the government were making the test for the purpose of recommending or prescribing a suitable guard this one, perhaps with others, should be most favourably regarded. Furthermore, the cost is very little-not more than $7. A practical engineer who saw it said that it could be manufactured in large quantities at $5 each. The government have not done their duty in regard to cattle-guards submitted for test. And I have no hesitation in saying that, as the government have spent'$6,942 in testing and paying the officers to make observations in connection with the test, the government should spend whatever small further sum might be necessary in order to publish the report. So long as the government keep the report secret, people will imagine that there is something wrong about it. The people should know how their money was expended and what the results were. "Whether those results are valuable or not valuable is a matter for further consideration.

It seems to me unnecessary to publish the report of the commission. ' The evidence has been taken and typewritten ; the report of the commissioners has been made ; and the whole now comes under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission wTho are the ones to finally settle this question.
Was not the test made under the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Emmer-son's) department and was not the report made to his department ?

Yes, and the whole business laid before the Railway Commission. At the time the commission began Mr. EMMERSON.
its work the Railway Department had jurisdiction and they naturally reported to the Railway Department, and about that time this parliament transferred jurisdiction from the Railway Department to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not know that my opinion under any circumstances would weigh with hon. gentlemen opposite, but it certainly would not have the weight of authority even if expressed, because the individual holding the position of Minister of Railways at this day is not clothed with jurisdiction with respect to this matter. It seems to me that in discussing a matter of this kind, we can hardly hope to accomplish great good through the department of Railways.

When I called attention to this matter, I did not suppose that it would be discussed for so long a time. Certainly, I shall not take many minutes in what further I have to say on the subject. The amount of money spent is not so very impiortant in itself.

As to whether the minister considered Mr. Holt slow, I am not concerned about that, except that I think it right to call attention to the fact of the investigation that took place ; and I think that if we take his own estimate we get a good gauge of the investigation that, as a matter of fact did take place. When Mr. Robertson retired in February the House was sitting. I was instructed by the Minister of Railways that the investigation was then practically completed. So we find that for four months afterwards the investigation continued, and with no practical benefit to anybody. Now with reference to the report, I do not think the minister has taken pains to ascertain

Low that matter stands. If this was a five cent report, being a matter of less than two folios, less than a page at all events, it might be well to have a copy. I have gone to the trouble of going over the matter, I find there is a lot of interesting matter in it but none that is very valuable. There are 9S8 pages of this stuff, and I think four-fifths of it is absolute rubbish. It is a repetition of letters, of copies of letters, of letters original and so forth. There is nothing in it of the nature of a report. You cannot tell where any report begins or where any report ends. The commissioners reported the evidence, but they have made no finding. If there is no report worth five cents a copy, there is no report at all that I could conscientiously recommend to have published because I would say that three or four hundred pages of evidence are reported but no finding as a result. I do not think the minister is right in the conclusion that this is a matter for the Railway Commission. I think it is a matter for his department. Mr. Robertson appears to be of no particular value in the matter, because he was allowed to leave before he had completed his duties, before he had made any report. We paid him for six months time, including Sundays, $905 and $S43.42 for expenses, and we got nothing from him in return. One of the commissioners, apparently, not only broke away from the commission, but he ceased operations and did not make any report. The House does not enjoy the advantage of appreciating his opinion on the subject of cat-tie-guards. How is that serious defect ever to be remedied ? Does the hon. Minister of Railways think it ever can be remedied ?

Mr. Robertson was chiefly appointed for the purpose of taking evidence ; he was not a scientific man at 238
all, only an ordinary common sense business man.
Very common sense.
Well, I like to see good, genuine common sense men on such a commission, with the emphasis on the common,' and Mr. Robertson is such a man.

I am not reflecting on either of these gentlemen, I am discussing the methods which were pursued. If the only duty of the commissioners was to take evidence, it would strike one who was not familiar with the technical way of dealing with these commissioners, that perhaps one could have done it as well as two-that' would seem to follow from the minister's remarks. Might I inquire whether any marked difference was found in the efficiency of the commission after Sir. Robertson had ceased to co-operate with Mr. Holt ?
Mr. Robertson only ceased when Mr. Holt started in to draw up his report from the scientific point of view ; he studied the question from the scientific and mechanical side.

Have we not been robbed-I trust ' robbed ' is not too strong a word-of the aspect of the question presented from the common sense side to which my hon. friend has drawn attention ? As I understand it. Mr. Robertson was the common sense man of the commission, and the other gentlqman was the scientific man. If we are to have presented to parliament only the scientific side and not the common sense side, how are we to understand the latter side ? Is it likely that at any time in the near future the common sense side will be presented to us by Mr. Robertson ?

I may explain to my hon. friend that the people of the country and parliament can draw their own deductions from that common sense presentation of the evidence. I do not wish to have it crystallized here ; parliament is supposed to have a great amount of ordinary common sense, and I do not suppose we need it to be crystallized in a report.
Then do we understand that Mr. Robertson gave evidence himself ?

He took the evidence and arranged it. I want my hon. friend to understand me. Mr. Robertson arranged who should give evidence at the different points where the commission sat. Mr. Robertson attended to the business side of the commisssion and the other gentleman was as the scientific member of the commission, having scientific knowledge as an engineer. Mr. Roberston arranged where and when the meetings should be held, he was practically the chairman of the commission. They went from place to place taking this evid-



ence, and he has reported that for the benefit of parliament as I think for the benefit of the Railway Commission, because that is the tribunal which will have jurisdiction in the settlement of this matter.

The difficulty seems to be that although the common sense to which my hon. friend refers may have been crystallized in the ease of Mr. Robertson, parliament does not enjoy the advantage of having the crystals placed before it.
The evidence has been reported to the House.

I know. My hon. friend says that Mr. Robertson's common sense was valuable in connection with this evidence. To what can that amount unless Mr. Robertson is possessed of some intuition which enables him to select the proper persons to give the evidence? I suppose that any man possessing an ordinary knowledge of the difficulties that surround the construction of a cattle-guard could have taken this evidence in about one quarter of the time and at about one-tenth of the expense that has been incurred. As far as I can see the whole commission has rather degenerated into a humbug. The only advantage that the country enjoys is that of paying the expenses of these gentlemen during a very considerably greater period than one would reasonably have expected to be occupied in making this inquiry.

There is one question which the hon. minister did not answer. I did not notice it at the time but this ' common sense ' discussion has brought it up. Mr. Holt in claiming compensation does not present the same view as that of the hon. minster in regard to the common sense of the other commissioner. Mr. Holt claims that the whole weight of the matter fell on him, that he was the chief person engaged in the inquiry and that therefore he is entitled to greater compensation. That is a matter that we will have to leave to be decided later on when we get more light upon it. But, the hon. minister has not said whether he agrees with the suggestion which is more than once repeated in the correspondence of Mr. Holt, that the government were not in earnest, that the government did not want the work to be done, that the government were not serious in the matter and that he was serious. As to that I would like the hon. minister to answer. Does he agree with Mr. Holt in his suggestion that the government were not serious, or is he able to say that the insinuation that they were not serious has been repudiated by the government ? I object very decidedly to this expenditure considering that we have nothing in the nature of a report from Mr. Holt or from Mr. Robertson. Mr. Robertson did not pretend to Mr. EMMERSON.
make a report. He performed a service for the party in another capacity by dropping out of the commission entirely to contest an election in the interests of the Liberal party and for that service I suppose he is excused from making a report.
Railways and canals-Miscellaneous-railway statistics, including clerical assistance, notwithstanding anything in the' Civil Service Act, $2,500.
Are these statistics required to be collected under the new Railway Act.
This is the usual vote from year to year. These statistics are provided for in the Railway Act.

In connection with these statistics I would urge upon the hon. minister that the Railway Commission and his department should be more active in getting statistics. It' developed here only the other day that while the Railway Act requires railway companies to file their standard passenger rates-
They have until November to do it.

I know that because the commission gave them an opportunity as a result of my calling attention to their dereliction in connection with the matter. All these statistics that are called for under the Act should be made good immediately. I also want to point out for the information of the Railway Commission that all statistics bearing on railway questions and especially on railway tariffs ought to be in the hands of the commission and available for the public. Anything I desired to ascertain in connection with railway operations I have had to go out and collect myself at very considerable expense. Before this item passes I would like to bring a matter to the attention of the hon. minister and I might as well bring it up on this item as upon any other. I want to ask the hon. minister if he will be good enough to tell the committee about McLaren's Creek. Last year and the year before there were items in the estimates for the construction of a roadway across McLaren's Creek but the work was stopped. I do not find any item in the estimates at all this year. Last year the department sent up an embankment,

about balf way across the creek, but the [DOT]dredge was taken away and no more has been done since. I understand that a gentleman in the Senate who claims to exercise patronage in that riding interfered and had the dredge taken away. This was not done in the hon. minister's time so that if he does not know anything about the matter be can give me the information at a later stage.

My information Is that the department offered to pay one-third of the cost of making the roadway providing the municipality, or interested parties, paid the remainder. The department started in to do their work and they were ready to do it but the others would not and the department has delayed matters until those interested are willing to perform their part of the work. That is my information.

I presume I know as much about this matter as any person but I never heard a hint once before that the municipality were supposed to do something. The understanding was that the road was to be left in such a position that the municipality could finish it up. This is the first time that X ever heard that the government were to pay one-third and the municipality two-thirds of the cost. The municipality have no right to do any of it at all. Owing to the construction of the government dam at Bobcaygeon teams have to go two miles west and two miles back to the east again to reach Lindsay. If it were not for the government dam, the creek would be readily accessible. I do *not know where the hon. minister's information comes from. If there is any correspondence in the matter I would ask the hon. minister to bring it down or I will go over to the department and see it.
There is another matter that I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. minister and it is in regard to Pigeon river bridge at the mouth of Pigeon river. It was taken away by the ice last winter. Inasmuch as the Pigeon river will be open to navigation as soon as the Trent canal is completed I would ask the minister to have his engineer look into it and consider the advisability of having a swing bridge at that point.

Governor General's car, repairs and alterations, $2,000.

I would like to ask the minister how many of these so-called government cars there are. I see it stated in this morning's paper that the Minister of the Interior left in his private car on Saturday for Winnipeg. I remember seeing in one of the prominent newspapers last winter that one of the government cars had arrived in Winnipeg to bring a relative of the Minister of the Interior to Ottawa for Christmas.
That was a mistake.
I beg the hou. gentleman's pardon-it was not a mistake. One of the government cars left here and went to Winnipeg to bring a relative of the Minister of the Interior down to spend Christmas.
Brought his father down.

What I want to know from the minister is for what degree of relationship may the cars be sent ? What is the extent of the consanguinity, and how many of these private cars are there ? It will not do for the minister to say that these things are not done. I myself saw two government cars standing in the Union Station at Toronto, and there was not a minister in one of them. It was a party of ladies.

A pleasure excursion up the line ; and when an hon. member of this House dies, and his fellow members wish to attend his funeral, they have to pay for their own Pullman's. The government would not even provide a private ear to take the body of the late Mr. McCreary to Winnipeg. I thought it was simply disgraceful. These cars can always be got by any of the ministers or their friends who want to make a junketting trip through the country, making exhibitions of themselves, and laughing at the poor farmers sweating in the fields. And yet when a member of the minister's own party dies, his body is sent in a baggage car to the Northwest.
I think the hon. gentleman' language lis not within proper-bounds. The use of private cars is to-day just what it has been since there have been private cars.
No, no.

-I happen to know something about that. When a minister applies to the Department of Railways for a car, it is assigned to him and the department knows nothing about the purpose for which he wants it. The ministers do not own private cars. The Department of Railways and Canals has, I think, five official cars, of which two are at Ottawa, and if a minister wants one in connection with any business he may have in hand, and if it is in the yard here he gets it on his requisition. Beyond that the department has-no knowledge. I am sure the statement made by my hon. friend about junketting is simply a figure of speech. He wishes to convey an idea of a condition of things which does not exist, and I am sure that on reflection he will feel like withdrawing the statement.

My language is not at all overdrawn. I say to the minister that it is a scandal in his own party. Hon. members sitting on his own side of the House have objected to it in much stronger language than I have used. I may not repeat the language because it was in the shape of personal attacks on the ministers and their friends.
They used to call them small potatoes. I do not know what they call them now.

I will not repeat the language which was used by members of the minister's own party, because it would not be parliamentary. If it comes to a vote, they will fall into line, but in their hearts they condemn the misuse of the cars ; and on the occasion of the death of Mr. McCreary, when one of these cars might properly have been used to remove his body to Winnipeg, members of the hon. minister's own party were indignant when they learned that the body had been sent, in a baggage ear ; and some of those who went with it came very near being left behind and not reaching Winnipeg at all.

With respect to the statement of my hon. friend I would say that this is the first time I have known that there ever was a request made to the Department of Railways for a car to go to Winnipeg on the occasion of the much lamented death of Mr. McCreary. I never heard of it before. If any such request had been made. I am sure the Department of Railways would have been only too pleased to have met the wishes of Mr. McCreary's friends.

It seems to me very strange that the minister should require a request for a car under such circumstances. A prominent member of the Liberal party died practically in the House while in the service of his country, and his body was carried in a baggage car instead of one of the government cars being used for that purpose. As a matter of fact, several ministers were approached on the subject by the member for North Victoria, and each one said it was not in his department. It should not have been necessary for any request to have been made at all.
It is a wonder the hon. member did not mention it to the head of the Railway Department.

I rang up the office of the Minister of Railways half a dozen times at the request of some of his own friends. I was told that the minister was not there, but was at Council. Then I rang up the Privy Council office. The message was sent to the Prime Minister while the cabinet was In Council, and I do not know what became of it. I also rang up the office of the Minister of the Interior, and spoke to the deputy minister and several other officers of that department ; but nobody seemed to care enough about the matter to do anything. I spoke personally to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and he declined to Interfere. The sum and substance of it is that they had no more use for the late member of Selkirk, and they allowed his body to go to Winnipeg in a baggage car, while they kept the private cars for pleasure trips up and down the side lines.
