Is it true that some time last year one of these cars was sent from Moncton to California ? If so, for what purpose was it sent ?
What time does my hon. friend refer to ?
Say within the last two years. I think it was some time yast year.
Sir William Mulock had one of the cars to go to Mexico.
AVhat-Sir William Mulock, the farmer's friend ?
Is it the same gentleman who was sympathizing with the farmers in Ontario the other night, who was rolling over the country to Mexico in a private car ?
My hon. friend had such a quantity of sympathy to express that I do not know how Sir William Mulock could find opportunity to get a word in.
If Sir William Mulock were to die, his body ought to be sent home in a baggage car the same as Mr. Mc-Crearys. I would be quite satisfied to see him sent home that way.
How much money is invested in these private cars ?
These are practically the same ears as have been owned by the government since the early days.
No, the hon. gentleman is quite wrong in his history of these government ears.
I could not tell you the amount of money invested for that purpose.
There was only one government car in the old days and that was the ' Jamaica.'

They began with one.
iMr. BENNETT. And these magnates have five now. I suppose that is because the ministers have always lived in private

cars of their own. What do these cars cost on an average ?

I can tell my hon. friend that he is very much mistaken when he says the late government had only one private car. I remember at the time of the funeral of the late Sir John Thompson, down at Halifax, there were four different ministers who had private cars at the time, each one having a car of his own.
Is the hon. gentleman sure that those four carriages were owned by the government at the time ?
Quite certain.
What were the names ?
I could not tell you that. One of the cars now in use cost $4,500. Another one cost $9,500. The one bought for the Duke and Duchess cost $20,000.
Are you not building another private car ?
There is something in the estimates for the Governor General's car and I was going to explain that when I got the opportunity.
Is there not an item of $18,000 to build a new car ?
The Railway Commissioners will require a car if they have not already purchased one.
That is ordered now.
Whether they have actually ordered it or secured it I do not know.
How much is it to cost?
Mr. FO WhEfi. The hon. minister has not answered my question about that trip to California.
There was no trip .that I was aware of to California except the one to Mexico.
This private car was sent to Moncton in connection with Mr. Tiffin.
Mr. Tiffin is the general traffic manager and has an official car in which he travels on business. Whether he went in it as far as California or not, I am not in position to say.

Mr. Tiffin was away on leave for six months, and it was during that time he had this car. My information is that during those six months he had this car with a party of friends, and went to California in it at the expense of the people of Canada.
It would not be at the expense of the people.
The government own the car.
Yes, but if he took the car away on such a trip it would not be at the expense of the government.
Would he pay for haulage ?
That is a courtesy extended by railways.
What would he pay ?
He would pay his living in the car and all the expenses connected with it.
Which of the cars went to Mexico ?
I think it was car 109.
Is it not a fact that when private cars are used by other ministers than the Minister of Railways, the railway companies generally charge for the haulage ?
That is paid by the individual minister and not by the government. All the expenses are paid by the individual and he simply has the use of the car.	.
What is the charge per mile ?

I think my hon friend will find that the courtesy is extended by railways to a minister even on American roads. They extend the courtesy of haulage. I know they do in Canada. I think that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway never charge any of the ministers for transportation and the Intercolonial does not charge railway directors. Unfortunately these railway magnates do not go down over the Intercdlonial often enough, or they would realize better what a fine country we have down there.

I would not say a word about private cars. If the minister goes off on business, it is his duty to travel in a private car, but what irritated me was that at the very time when poor McCreary's body was sent away in a baggage car, I heard from Liberal members in this House

I am only sorry my hon. friend did not state the matter to me. All that would have been necessary would have been to mention the fact to me. I never heard a whisper of it. I regret that the suggestion did not occur to myself.
What is the name of the cal built for tlie Duke and Duchess of York ?
Is that the one the minister uses for his own private use ?

Do not put it in that way. It is the car that has been used by

the Minister of Railways, and X have the temerity to use it now.
Perfectly right.
I understood that the hon. minister went to Nova Scotia with a party of friends. I presume he had oar No. 109 ?
That is the car I had.
What private oars were there in connection with the government railways and used by the ministers in 1890 ?
A return was brought down about that during this session. X have not the papers here.
The minister might ash his deputy for the information.
There is one additional ear now over those that existed in 1896 in connection with the Department of Railways.
Was there a Governor General's car previous to 1896 ?

Yes ; that is the one that has cost so much to repair. It is called the ' Victoria.' It was provided for the use of the Governor General. His Excellency has reported time and again within the last two or three years that it was much out oi repair. It seemed to toe cheaper to purchase a new car than to incur this annual expense for repairs. In a few minutes I shall ash the committee to vote $18,000 for a new car for the Governor General.
Then what is this $2,000 for 1
For the changes necessary to make it into some other kind of a car.
As a private car ?
No ; it is not so intended.
Wre have one car now in addition to those we had in 1S96, and when this $18,000, to which the minister refers, is voted, that will make a second additional car.	.

No ; that will put the 'Victoria' out of commission, so that there will not be an additional car.
Mr. INGRAM, Then why spend this. $2,000 r If that amount is spent on a car, it must be in order to keep the car in use.

This.item was put in last February, of course, before the determination had been reached to build a new car. Since then, talking with His Excellency and others who are interested, it seemed to me it would be better to vote money for a new car ; and my idea is to utilize the old car in some way in connection with the Intercolonial. If that cannot be done the money will not he spent.
Then it is not true, as was raid a few minutes ago, that this will make an additional car which will become available for the Intercolonial or officials of the government ?
My idea is to make it into a passenger car in connection with the Intercolonial.

The government is going to provide an additional car for the Governor General and also a car for the Railway Commission. Besides this they have one additional car since 1896. That makes three new cars since 1896.
In the four cars which he says were owned by the government prior to 1896, does the minister include the Governor General's car ?
No.
What were the four cars ?
My memory is not good enough to give the hon. gentleman that information.
I do not expect the hon, minister to be able to remember details of that kind. But he has his officials beside him, and surely they can tell him.
They do not remember.
Will the hon. minister tell me that the deputy minister does not know how many private cars there are on the road ? Why, any school boy living along the road can tell that.

I may tell the hon. minister that as long ago as 1892 there was an old oar that stood down here on the siding that was used by the ministers of that time during an election tour. I think it was the only car around here. I do not think the minister can be allowred to make the statement that there were four cars at that time unless he gives us the names.
There was the ' Ottawa,' the ' Cumberland,' a car known as No. 84, and another car whose name or number T do not know.
"Where were the four cars kept ?

Two here constantly- the 1 Ottawa ' and the 1 Cumberland.'
Sir. FOWLER, And where were the four in commission ?	[DOT]
I gave the exact information to answer that question, but I have not the notes at hand, and I cannot remember.	-
I think we ought to be able to get the exact number of these cars, there are not so many of them. The min-

ister says that in 1896 there were four cars ; I want to know whether those four are still in commission, and if so, where are they used. For instance, at Moncton-as 1 understand it, Mr. Pottinger, the general manager,'"has a car of his own. Mr. Tiffin also has a car of his own. Are there any other cars kept at Moncton belonging to a particular official ?

We have two cars at Moncton, one No. 75, used by the general manager and the general superintendent, the other, the number of which I do not know, is used by the traffic manager. Then we have one used by the deputy minister, which "was also used by the deputy minister previous to 1896 ; that is known as the ' Ottawa ". Then we have the car known as the ' Montreal I do not know her number. In addition we have the ear No. 109, the one that has been used by ministers. That makes five, and as I stated there were four previous to 1896 ; the sixth is the Governor General's car.
The ' Ottawa used by the deputy minister, is that also used by members of the government ?

It is still known as the deputy minister's car, and is used largely in the business of the department. When it is not engaged on that business it is used by members of the government. When ministers want a car and send in a requisition to the department, if the other car is not ready that one is taken. On the occasion this last winter when the Postmaster General was ill car 109 was used by him in going to Mexico.
Do I understand it is the intention of the minister to condemn the present Governor General's car and use it as a passenger car on the Intercolonial ?
That is my idea, to convert it into a passenger car.

I understand that these cars are made with compartments, and it would seem to involve a good deal of sacrifice to make that change. But I would point out that we have this condition of things, that the estimates are brought down with a vote of $2,000 to repair the Governor General's car ; we have no objection to that, if it is necessary.

I may explain that we put that item in the estimates when it was supposed that the car would continue to be used as the Governor General's. Since then I have changed the estimates and put in an additional amount of $18,000 for a new car ; and I have decided to change the present car used by the Governor General into a passenger ear for the Intercolonial, probably a parlour car.
That appears to be a second thought on the part of the minister, we must follow events as they have occurred.
That is no second thought at all.

We discussed this item at considerable length before the minister made this intimation, we are discussing this $2,000 item for the repair of the Governor General's car, and just now the minister announces that it is not for that purpose at all. Then I think I am justified in assuming that probably it is an afterthought when he says that it is to be turned into a passenger car. Now I venture to predict, having regard to circumstances as they have occurred, that it is highly probable that the minister will again change his mind, and that the car will be devoted to the same class of service as the other cars that are denominated official cars, and that it will make one more car available for members of the administration. It seems to be impossible to ascertain just how many official cars we have. It is remarkable that it should be impossible to know clearly by name and number their proper official designation. and how many cars we have. An inquiry was made a month ago upon this question, it was referred to several times in the House, and the minister has sitting at his elbow the deputy minister, and yet we cannot get explicit information as to what cars we have in the service of the government. So far as I understand, we have the Ottawa, the Montreal, the Cumberland, we have No. 109 for the Minister of Railways, we have No. 75 and No. 34. I think we can now safely conclude that after the purchase or construction of another official car for the Governor General, we will have seven or eight cars at all events.
Are these two new cars to be built in Canada ?
There is only one car to be constructed, the Governor General's car. which is to be constructed in Canada.
I think he said the commissioners had ordered a car for themselves.

They purchased a car.
I think they got it for immediate use, from the Pullman Company.
Where are they going to have this new car built ?

I do not think I should tell my hon. friend at this moment. I have an offer from people in Canada, but I am not prepared to accept it until the vote is passed. However, I have stated that it will be built in Canada. I have an .offer that will enable us to have it built in Canada within the sum mentioned in the item.
Was this car 109 built In Canada ?
No.
Did the minister authorize this expenditure on the part of the Railway Commissioners ? On what authority did they order it or purchase it ?

Under the authority of a vote. It was necessary for them to have an official car for the Railway Commission. They were obliged to go to Toronto and other points in the west, and there was no car in the service of the Department of Railways and Canals that would accommodate them. There are three commissioners, and they have their officials with them. It is quite a large party. They require at least three rooms, one for each commissioner. There is no car at present available, not one of the cars has that number of rooms and it is therefore necessary to have such a car for the Railway Commissioners. Efforts were made to purchase one from the railway companies in Canada if they had any available but none could he found that would at all suit the requirements. The Railway Commissioners have assignments for holding meetings in the west at very many points and they require to leave here at a very early date.
I do not think the hon. minister has answered the question as to where their authority came from. Is there a sum of money placed at their disposal to be used as they see fit ?
Not at their disposal, but, at their disposal with the authority of the Governor in Council.
What is the amount ? Is it unlimited ?

No. There was an amount placed in last year's estimates for the expenses in connection with the Railway Commission. The expenditure of that had to be authorized by the Governor in Council and they have received authority to purchase a car for $20,000.
The authority of the Governor in Council ?

We never anticipated that the item of $20,000 passed last year would go without the authority of parliament for the purpose of purchasing a car. It was for incidental expenses, and the purchase of a private car was scarcely contemplated. I would think that it would cost them at least $20,000 to provide a private car suitable for their purposes.
My hon. friend, will admit that they should have an official car.
Is not this car, which I understand is so beautifully fited up, sufficient for them V
It is not large enough.
How many officials do they carry with them ?
They have at least one engineer and they have a number of secretaries.
Does each one have a secretary '!
Not each one. They have one secretary and they require a stenographer, and I think they will require a legal assistant.
Have they any yet ?
I think they will have one.
Will they take a chaplain with them V
Is my hon. friend open for such a position ?

I think this commission ought to have a car but I think it is a reflection on Canada and the industries of Canada that that ear should be built outside of this country. Some arrangement should be made whereby the car should be built in this country. They require a first-class car as far as accommodation is concerned. I do not begrudge them that, but it is a reflection on our country and on our manufacturers that we should not be able to build that car in this country. Some provision surely could have been made until such time as a Canadian built car could be placed at the disposal of the Railway Commission.

When I asked tenders from Canadian car builders for the Governor General's car there was only one concern in Canada that was willing to undertake it. All the car men were written to and asked for prices and the firm to which I have referred were not in a position to undertake it until next autumn. That is the position and it is necessary to have the car for these people at once. If you hired a car from the Pullman Car Company you would expend in their exorbitant charges for rental in a few months almost enough to build a car. Therefore, in the interest of economy it was deemed advisable and necessary to buy this car elsewhere.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Governor General's car-repairs and alterations, $2,000.
Mr. .1. D. REID. As I understand there are five of these government cars besides the Governor General's car which makes six altogether.

I explained that there are two cars here, two at Moncton, and the

one generally used by the Minister of Railways No. 109, although it is not exclusively used by him at all times.
I). REID. Then there is one now to be supplied to the Railway Commission.
I think that car has been arranged for and that they are going west within a day or two.
That then makes six cars, besides the Governor's car.

If my hon. friend wants to include the Governor General's car that will be six. Let us understand it; I do not wish to hide anything in respect to it. I am speaking of government cars here and at Moncton under the charge of the department. There are live of such ears. The Governor General's car and the Railway Commissioner's car are not under the control of the Railway Department.
Then there are seven private ears used by the government and the Railway Commission ?
Do you not think you had better say official cars, offices on wheels ?
Very well, official cars. Do I understand that there are only two of these ears used by Ministers of the Crown ?

There are none of them assigned to Ministers of the Crown. Ministers occasionally require the use of a car and they make application to the Department of Railways and Canals, and if there is one available it is assigned to their use for a particular trip.
Could the minister give me any information as to the cost to the country of maintaining each of these cars ?
I gave that information to the House in answer to a question.

I wish to enter my protest against the government sending Canadian money to the United States to purchase a private car to be used by the Railway Commission. The minister stated that last year $20,000 was voted to be expended by the Railway Commission.
I did not name that amount because I did not have it before me.
Would the hon. gentleman say what the amount was ?
I cannot from memory.

There was an amount voted last year to be placed at the disposal of the Railway Commission. As I understand a request was made to the Governor in Council for a private car to cost $20,000 for the use of the Railway Commission and the Governor in Council gave their sanction to that amount being expended.
In last year's estimates.

I think it was the duty of the Governor in Council to stipulate that the car should be purchased within the limits of Canada. My hon. friend has said that an advertisement was published asking for tenders fqr the purchase of a car and that the only reply-

Not for that car. I said that as respects that car an effort was made to find out whether such a car could be secured in Canada at all. It was impossible to get it in time or in fact before next fall or winter. So far as the Governor General's car was concerned, it was not required immediately. I have received an offer from one Canadian manufacturer to furnish such a ear to be delivered sometime during the present fiscal year, but the car required by the Railway Commissioners, could not now be furnished at all in Canada and it was necessary to get one that was already constructed.
So it would be if we could get it.

The government should have stipulated when voting $20,000 for a car for the Railway Commission that that car should be purchased within the limits of Canada. The minister says that one could not be secured before the fall or winter. Even if that be correct-and I accept the statement and say it is correct-I say that the Railway Commission should have used one of the cars that is at the disposal of the . government now. There is a car for the Governor General, a very expensive car, which was constructed by the government a short time ago at a cost of $20,000.

I have explained to my hon. friend that that car is not large enough for the Railway Commission. They require for their purpose a car containing three rooms. I think my hon. friend will take that statement as being correct.
I accept the hon. gentleman's statement ; I am not disputing that at all ; but the Railway Commission is not travelling through this country all the time, but only occasionally.	[DOT]
They want to be away two or three months in the west, and they need a car. They should have gone at an earlier date than the present.	-
When was the commission appointed ?
In February last.

The minister and the government knew full well that the commission would require a car. I am not saying whether the car already constructed is suitable for the requirements of the commission or not; but I do say that a car that would have been suitable could have been ordered, and if the commission had to wait five or six or even twelve months to secure the construction of that car in Canada, they should have done so and they could in the meantime have used one of the cars already at the disposal of the government. I do not think the people of Canada will sanction the expenditure of money in this way. Here is a Canadian Railway Commission travelling through western Canada in a car on which is written, ' manufactured in the United States,' when they should be travelling in a car on which would be written. ' made in Canada,' which is the popular term now. I say the government did not discharge their full duty to the people when they voted that $20,000 should be spent on a car without stipulating that the money should be spent in Canada. The hon. minister says they could not wait. Well, there are a good many people in Canada who have to wait, and if the Railway Commission do not meet any greater obstacle than that of having to wait five or six months for a car, they will get through their duties very easily. I object, and I think the Canadian people will object, to the government setting this example by passing an Order in Council placing at the disposal of the Railway Commission $20,000 of Canadian money to be spent in the United States.

The minister has referred two or three times to the fact that an appropriation was made last session for the use of the Railway Commission. I ask him now, what was the amount of the appropriation placed to the credit of the Railway Commission last year ?

I venture to say that not one dollar of that appropriation was intended to be used for the purchase of a car, and I call the attention of the minister and the members of the government present to that abuse of their power. There was absolutely no excuse for it. The minister says none of the cars owned by the government are large enough. X am not prepared to say that is not correct. It may be, and I think very likely is so, that some different accommodation may be required in the end from that furnished by any cars at present owned by the government. But we have five government cars, and if one of these cars was not sufficient to accommodate these gentlemen, two of them wquld have been sufficient, and should have been assigned to their service for the time being rather than that this large amount
of money should be devoted to this purpose without the sanction of parliament, and the money sent to the people of the United States-the manufacturers of Canada deprived of that money, and, a great deal worse than that, the fact advertised throughout Canada and the United States that such a car could not be manufactured in Canada. The minister has brought forward no reasonable justification for the action of the department or the government in this matter. It was not necessary for these gentlemen to have absolutely convenient accommodation upon this trip to the west. They are not going to take evidence or hold investigations in any unfrequented places along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway or other railways. They are going to hold investigations at the large centres, and it was not necessary that they should be able to lodge upon their car during the time of those investigations. It would have been reasonable for these gentlemen for the present to have had one official car at their disposal. Others could very well have been accommodated in a state-room upon a Canadian Pacific Railway pullman car ; and the other officials, the engineer and others, could have obtained very fair accommodation upon the pullman cars of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Therefore there is no justification whatever for the government having appropriated this money to this purpose. I submit in the first place that it is absolutely unconstitutional because the money was not voted by parliament for that purpose ; and, in the second place, even if it had been voted for that purpose, it is a very poor principle on which the government has acted, in diverting the money to the United States, to the pecuniary loss and the great detriment of the people of Canada.
How does this car compare with the car built for the Duke and Duchess ?
It is a larger car, and has more accommodation.
What is the difference in length ?

I cannot tell, because it is the Railway Commission which sees to the dimensions of the car and the arrangement of it. It has better accommodation for a greater number of people than the car purchased for the Duke and Duchess. The car purchased for the Duke and Duchess is not a oar that surpasses every other.
A very comfortable car.
As my hon. friend says, it is a very comfortable car, and I have no wish to decry it.
By whom was this car built ?

By the Pullman Car Company. There is no concern in Canada
75 07

at this moment in a position to take an order for a car of that character. They are not fitted up for the purpose. There is only one concern which contemplates doing that business, and they are not in the position to do it now. They do not furnish pullman sleepers in Canada.
They may not furnish pullman sleepers, but they can build a car plenty good enough for the class of railway commissioners we have.
They will not undertake to do it.
They are not given much opportunity.

Surely my hou. friend will not make that statement in the face of what X have just said. X have said to my hon. friend that they are not in a position to do it, and I say that from their own statement. I hope my hon. friend will not show me the discourtesy of insisting that they have not had the opportunity.
Who are these people to whom the hon. gentleman refers ?
The Crossen Company, of Cobourg ; the Rhodes, Curry Company, of Amherst; the Rathbun Company, of Deseronto. These are the only three concerns that make cars in Canada.
Did they give any statement as to the limit of time they would take ?

They were asked whether they could tender for any cars. One said they were not in a position ; the *others said they would not accept the order at all. The Rhodes, Curry Company said they were not now in a position, but that they would place themselves in a position, so that by next fall they could undertake the construction of such cars.

Evidently if the government had not been in such a hurry, and the ministers been willing to make a little saeri flee and travel as ordinary people do, we would have sufficient cars to accommodate the commission. There is another question I would ask. This car has been made by the Pullman Car Company, of Chicago. I presume that the company will have a travelling advertisement on it. Will their name be on this oar, and where it was made and the date ?
I presume so. I have not inquired, but I observe that on cars throughout the country the name of the maker is always painted somewhere.
I would suggest that the minister should have that painted in black, as a sign of mourning for the poor Canadians who cannot build a car for the commissioners.
Will the $20,000 come our of the $40,000 voted last year ?
Yes.

I have a copy of the Railway Act. Subsection 4, section 21, refers to the expenditure of money. I see under this subsection that :
The salaries or remunerations of all such officers, clerks, stenographers, messengers, and appointees, and all the expenses of the hoard of, and incidental to, the carrying out of this Act, including all actual and reasonable travelling expenses of the commissioners, secretary, and of such appointees or members of the staff of the board as may be required by the board, to travel, necessarily incurred in attending to the duties of their office, shall be paid monthly out of moneys to be provided by parliament.
Does that clause cover the expenditure ?

I think so. It is to be
paid out of the vote last session of $40,000.
Under this particular clause, does the hon. minister think the government are justified in making that payment ?
I think the government is justified in paying for the car as an incidental expense connected with the Railway Commission, and it has already been provided and paid for.
Has the item passed the Auditor General ?
I could not say.

The only words I see in the clause that possibly could attach to it are these : ' travelling expenses incurred in attending to the duties of their office.' Surely he will not contend that under those the government are entitled to take $20,000 out of the $40,000 voted by parliament and use it to build this car. Assuming, for the sake of argument, that last year the government stated that $20,000 of this vote was intended to be for the purchase of a car, does the hon. minister assume that it would have gone without protest ?
I am sure I would not assume that. I do not know of anything that would go without protest, but I assume it would have gone all right.
I do congratulate the minister on his frankness. He says anything will go with the majority of the House.
Any reasonable proposition which ought to go.

In the face of the fact that the government have five private cars for which the people have no use, is it not the height of extravagance to buy another one V When one minister wants to bring a relative from Manitoba, he sends a private car for him. Another one takes a private

car on a jaunt to California. Another minister takes a private car for a trip to Mexico.
No minister took one to California.

When the mnnister was asked about one of these private cars being sent to Manitoba to bring the relatives of one of his colleagues down here, he knew nothing about it. When he was asked with reference to one minister or his family taking a private car to California, he knew nothing about it. The people are long-suffering, but there must be a limit to their endurance. Had the minister stated last year that five of these private cars were standing on sidings not being used at all-
I do no think the hon. gentleman is justified in making that statement.
I mean for the purposes of the government.
Three of them are in use by the officials of the Intercolonial.

One was used by the .Postmaster General to go to Mexico on a trip ; another was handed over to the tender mercies of a government official to go to California ; while another was used for one of the ministers to send for one of his relatives to come to Ottawa. There were times probably, when these gentlemen did not travel in this style ; when they were pleased to take the ordinary cars of 'which the train was made up. An hon. gentleman behind me suggests 'first-class'; but they did not always get up to that even, perhaps. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) laughs. I was in this House when that hon. gentleman was on this side. I will give him credit for not having been so blatant about the use of private cars as was the present minister the Postmaster General (Sir William Mu-lock) and some others. But those hon. gentlemen scorned the use of private cars. We remember how, when the present Prime Minister attained office in 1896, he was offered a private car to come to Ottawa, but he said he preferred to travel in the ordinary car as a plain democrat. And this was heralded all over the country. This will all be interesting and amusing to the people of Ontario. And we remember that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said that so far as the Conservative party were concerned they could not elect a man in Quebec at all

Will the hon. minister allow me to finish the sentence ?-and if one of them did get here it would be through an accident or a mistake.
Mr. B'lELDING. That is right.

The hon. minister lost his head as he was applauded vociferously by his supporters. And perhaps that statement will be heard of in the province of Ontario and other parts of this Dominion.
