And when the people remember that he took one of these cars belonging to the country-and, forsooth the best one, the one impregnated with the air of royalty- and, as 1 a democrat to the hilt ' junketed off down to Mexico, while another car is sent by one of the ministers to bring his father from the city of Winnipeg, they will realize where these ' democrats ' are to-day. And. so far as the statement of the Minister of Finance is concerned, if he will refer to 1 Hansard ' he will find there in black and white-that if a Conservative were elected from the province of Quebec, it would be the result of an accident or of a mistake.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That applies to all the provinces.

The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will be making a tour of Ontario within the next two months. He will have all the influence of this government behind him ; he will have all the influence of the local government behind him, and he will have all the influence of the Grand Trunk Pacific behind him ; and I think he will come back from that province with the same stinging rebuke of defeat that was administered to him in 1900.
New car for the Governor General, $18,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Carried.
Provided that it is made in Canada.
We understand that the minister tells us that this eighteen-thousand dollar car is to be made in Canada ?
I stated that the Governor General's car was to be built in Canada. I hope it is not necessary to repeat it more than once.
Will the hon. minister say where it will be built ?

I am not in a position to make a statement on that point until the offer is accepted. Perhaps my hon. friend may infer from what I have-already stated.
Railways and canals-chargeable to collection of revenue-canals-staff and repairs, $789,562.

I propose to bring up again the question of the payment of the

employees of the Welland canal which I brought up last session and. on their behalf to try to find out some reason from the government why it is that they have not been paid an increase. Last session, when this item or a similar item was under discussion, I took some trouble to place before the House and the government the position of the loclcmasters and tenders and the bridge masters and tenders upon the Welland canal. We received a promise from the then Minister of Railways that the matter would be given attention and that a supplementary estimate would be brought down. A supplementary estimate was brought down, and a statute was passed which provided for an increase of twenty-five cents a day on the canals throughout Canada. Yet, strange to say the employees of the Welland canal have been told that they are not to get the increase and tney have not yet received it. Though it is a repetition of what was said last year, 1 propose to state the position of these men, who, I think, are entitled to their increase in an additional way to that in which they were entitled to it last year. Last year they were entitled to it on the merits and this year they are entitled to it technically as well, if I understand anything about the meaning of a statute. These men earn from about $360 to about $400 a year. Last year I pointed out, and I may now repeat-as we have done a good deal of business and the matter may have been forgotten-;that the salaries of civil servants, who make about as many thousands as these men make hundreds, were increased on the ground that the cost of living had increased and that they needed more to support themselves in the scale of living to which they had been accustomed. To-night, I have pointed out. and I repeat, that you are beginning at the wrong end. If the cost of living has increased and you are going to increase salaries, you ought to begin with the men who get three or four hundred dollars and not with the men who get three or four thousand. At all events if you do not begin there you should finish there-the men who make only three or four hundred a year certainly should be increased if increases are to be made on any ground. Now the circumstances of these men on the Welland canal have not been well understood by this government, I fancy, or they would have increased the wages years ago. I find that these men have not had an increase -though it seems to have been supposed that they have had-since what is called the New Welland canal was built twenty-five or. more years ago. The officers, men who get from $1,500 to $2,000 and so on, have had their salaries increased.
This government appears to think that when a man gets a good salary it is a sufficient reason for increasing it. whereas the man who gets a mere pittance of a few hun-Mr. LANCASTER.
dred dollars a year must remain at that figure. I find also that these men are required to have a certain amount of skill in locking these vessels through the canal, and that they do have skill is shown by the fact that there have been very few accidents on that canal ; Still they get less than ordinary labourers do. The question was asked this session by some hon. gentlemen opposite. what wages were paid to the labourers on the Soulanges and Lachine canals and on the St. Louis lock, and the answer, as found on page 5582, made by the Minister of Railways, was, that the ordinary labourers are getting $1.50 a day on these canals. These labourers however do not require any skill or any knowledge about the mechanism of the locks and no particular fitness for that position at all. Now what do the Welland canal employees get ? The labourers get $1.50 for nine hours work. I am not finding fault with that, that is about the same as labourers get on other canals. But I am speaking about lock tenders and bridge tenders upon the Welland canal, those men who are not employed the year round, and still are prevented from getting any other lucrative employment outside the canal. They work only about eight months in the year, and they get $45 a month.
Some of them take their turn at employment during the winter season.

They get very little that way. I am safe in saying that their average salary does not exceed $360 u year. Now these lock tenders and bridge tenders are paid 144 cents per hour, while the ordinary labourer gets 10 j cents per hour. In other words, men who have no skill get two cents an hour more than lock tenders and bridge tenders who are required to have skill. Now I do not wish the minister to think that it is only these men who are concerned ; the whole country is concerned in having properly qualified and therefore reasonably paid men upon these locks. The other night when we were discussing railway estimates, the Postmaster General saw fit to interject the remark that the Welland canal employees were appointed for political reasons and that I might expect these men would vote against me. Now I want the minister to understand that I don't care anything about that. If a man votes against me I still want him to be paid a fair wage while he is working for the King. I don't want the minister to think that he is pleasing me if ho does not raise the salaries of these men, oven if every one of them voted against me. No matter how they exercise their franchise, as long as they are kept in the service, I want to see them paid a reasonaole price for the work they do. The whole country is concerned in these men being properly

paid, because if you do not pay men reasonably well you cannot expect reasonably good service from them. These men lock and unlock not only bridges for railway trains, but bridges over highways for vehicles of all kinds ; therefore they are entrusted to a certain extent with the lives of many people. and the travelling public upon both the railways and highways as well as ships are concerned in having this work properly done and these men properly paid.
Now the wages of workmen on the Intercolonial are higher than those on this canal. During this present session the minister took good care to tell us on the 7th of June, in Introducing his estimates, that he had increased the wages of the Intercolonial Railway employees, and he took to himself much credit for doing so. He also increased the wages of the men on the Prince Edward Island Railway, giving as a reason that living expenses have greatly increased. Now the canal employee getting $45 a month for a day of twelve hours, only gets 14* cents an hour, working twenty-six days in the month. If they do a little extra work on Sundays, they get paid for that, so it is fair to leave that out of the discussion. I don't think anyway that they ought to be called upon to work Sundays. Now if they work twenty-six days in the month for eight months, and they have no chance to earn anything extra worth speaking of. that means from $360 to $400 a year. But their living expenses have increased just as well as they have increased for the m-ani who is getting $2,500 or $3,000 a year. If the latter suffers from increased cost of living he only has to economize in luxuries, he does not need to economize in the necessaries of life. He may have to buy less opera house tickets, lie may have to take a shorter vacation or a less expensive vacation 'in summer, and forgo a few little pleasures of that kind. But the man who gets $3(30 or $400 a year has got to forego probably shoes for his children to go to school in, he has got to forego perhaps fuel and clothes to keep them warm in winter ; he has to economize in the absolute necessities of life. Last year I made a plea on behalf of these men, and the then acting Minister of Railways said he would consider it. An estimate was brought down, that estimate was made a statute, and now I am curious to know, and so are the lock tenders on these canals, why that statute has not been carried out. because it has not been carried out by the government. We know of this government having made pledges and having broken them and apparently thinking it was not a serious thing. We have got a step further now. We have a statute of the Dominion passed last year providing that these men should have an increase of 25 cents a day and they have not received it. I refer the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to chapter 4 of the statutes of 1903
wnich is the Appropriation Act (No. 4) of last session and page 92 of this statute where he will find under the heading of ' Collection of Revenue-Railways and Canals ' and under the sub-head of ' Canals" the following :
Generally-increase of 25 cents per diem to the wages of lockmasters, lockmen, bridge men and ferry men of the various canals, $37,000.
There is the statute providing that the increase shall take place. These men have been told, that, notwithstanding the fact that the Act came into force in October last, they are not to get this increase, that this government are not going to give it to them. I do not know where this government stand upon this matter. We got a statute passed providing for an increase of 25 cents a day to lockmasters, lockmen, bridgemen and ferrymen on the various canals. None is named. If that money is paid to the men on one canal it must be paid to the Welland canal employees. I am told that it had been stated by the superintendent of the canal, or at least it was stated on the streets of St. Catharines, that the government had said that this increase was not intended to apply to the Welland canal. If the government meant that' they should have said so in their statutes. After I went home last session and told these men that this statute had been passed they were entitled to believe that they were going to get that 25 cents a day. If they are not going to get it no one should get it. There is no canal mentioned ; there is none excluded. There is no authority on the statute for paying that 25 cents a day to anybody if there is no authority for paying to the lockmasters, lockmen, bridgemen and ferrymen on the Welland canal. These men knowing that this statute was passed, knowing that this is the law of the land, knowing that this is the only way you can make a law that is binding on this government, surely had a right to expect that they would get the benefit of it. But, it seems that this government are not going to be bound by a statute although this is the only way in which we can bind the government to anything. This statute provided that these men on the various canals should receive an increase of 25 cents a day, yet, notwithstanding the fact that this statute has been passed, they are not getting the increase and they are told by the authorities that the statute does not apply to the Welland canal. On behalf of these men I urge their claim for a twofold reason. To begin with, on the merits of the case, they should have an increase. They are getting the same pay that they had twenty years ago and they so forcibly brought their claim to the attention of the government last year that this statute was passed. If the statute gave them 25 cents a day they ought to get it. I stand for the whole of Canada although I am speaking

particularly atoout the men of the Welland canal because they are the men who are complaining to me about this matter. I say they should have the same rate of pay as men on the other canals. Men who do the same work on the Soulanges canal or on the Sault Ste. Marie canal should get the same pay. I do not say that a man should get higher pay simply because he is on the Welland canal. Not at all. I want to give every Canadian workman the same increased pay wherever he may happen to be in Canada. I think it is fair to suppose that the expenses of living has increased in the same proportion in all parts of Canada and I therefore say that all these men are entitled to an increase of 25 cents a day. Whether it has been paid on the other canals or not, I do not know, but I do say that if this increased rate of pay has been given on the other canals and not on the Welland canal the government are doing something which the statute does not authorize them to do. The statute, as I have said before, applied generally to all of the canals and this increase of 25 cents per day should be paid upon all of them. The case of these men is certainly meritorious and I believe that the government would be in a very difficult position if one of these men who had worked on this canal since last session proposed to sue the government for this increased pay. I do not know how he could get a stronger contract than the statute. I cannot understand why the benefit of this statute has been withheld from them. It may be that the government-I hope not in the face of the meritorious ease which they were able to present-intended to make an exception of the Welland canal, because of the political stripe of the representative who comes here, but I do not think this government would punish these men in that way. These men do the work just the same. It is not their fault that a supporter of the Conservative party comes to this House and I do not believe until I receive better advice that such would be the reason for excepting the Welland canal. I do not know whether the government intended to except the Welland canal, but if they did they did not draw their statute properly. If they did not intend to pay the increase to the men on the Welland canal, and if they did intend to pay it on the other canals they should have made a different law, while, if they intended that all these men should be entitled to the benefit of the statute then the statute [DOT] certainly carries out their intention. These men have a right to expect that the government meant what the statute says. Some of these men, when I got home last autumn -not my political supporters-told me that if they had not got that increase they would have resigned because the pay was altogether too small, and they could not support their wives and children upon it. I told them that they had the increase, that the Mr. LANCASTER.
statute said so. Was I correct in that statement? If the government intended to-except the Welland canal they should have worded that statute differently. These men are not the drawers of the statute, they are not in parliament, they cannot discuss these things with the government; they can only go by the phrase that is in the statute and assume, that, this statute having been passed providing for an increase of pay generally, they would get their increase. I could not imagine any reason why the government should have not paid them. The failure of the government to pay them has resulted in my promising that when the-House did meet and when we got the right item in the estimates I would question the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, or whoever happened to be in his place, and give them the answer that the government might make as to why this increase has been withheld from them and I shall await that answer with a great deal of curiosity.

The explanation of that is that for twenty years, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) has said, or at least for a number of years, the employees on the Welland canal and on the Sault Ste. Marie have enjoyed the privilege of drawing $1.50 a day for their services. On the other canals they only received $1.25 a day.
Those are the labourers. I am talking about the lockmasters, lockmen, &c.

No, that is the class of men to which the hon. gentleman has been referring, so I am informed by the deputy minister. I get my information from him as to what occurred in the past. Provision was made in the estimates of last year to equalize to make uniform the payment to the classes of employees named in this item to which my hon. friend has made reference. I have a great deal of sympathy with all that my hon. friend has said as to the desirability of paying the employees on these canals the highest possible wage consistent with the compensation that men under similar circumstances are getting from private corporations. Of course it is difficult to make a comparison as between canals and other employments, because we have no precisely similar occupations. In the railway branch of the department the Intercolonial Railway can equalize the pay received by the men to that received under similar circumstances on other railways in Canada. That rule has been followed. This clas? of employees all over the canal systems in Canada receive the same pay. Whether that was right or wrong, that was made uniform and I am informed by the deputy that that was the object of the vote of last year. I am not just as familiar with the appointments of the men on the canals as I have been with regard to the railways,

but I shall make It a point to look into the matter. I admit that the cost of living has increased not so much by the increase in the cost of material as by the fact that what were the luxuries of a few years ago have become the necessities of to-day. That applies to all classes and all conditions of men in Canada today. My hon. friend says the labourers are paid 2i cents per hour more than the lock-masters. That is perhaps not making as fair an argument as my hon. friend wished to do. The labourers work nine hours per diem and get $1.50 per day. The others are on duty 12 hours it is true but they get $1.50 per day. I am not prepared to deny the contention of my hon. friend that men in that position should receive a higher wage than labourers employed elsewhere on the canal. It may be that they should ; that is a matter which I shall investigate personally, and I shall be only too glad to have a readjustment made so that the men will get what will be a fair compensation for their services. That is the principle adopted on the Intercolonial Railway and that course will be followed while I am in charge of the department in regard to the canals. When this matter was under discussion last session the Minister of Finance said :
If they are now receiving less than $1-50 per day, they will he increased to $1.50. This applies to all the canals except the Welland and the Sault Ste. Marie canals, the men on which had previously received an advance.
Thus it was explained at the time that this $37,000 was required in order to bring the standard wage on the other canals up to the wages on the Sault Ste. Marie and the Welland canals. This explanation of it accords with the explanation given me by the deputy minister and chief engineer who is more familiar with the details than I am. However, while that entirely refutes the argument of my hon. friend that any unfair action was taken by the government against the men on the Welland canal the other contention of my hon. friend that these men are worthy of a higher wage will certainly have consideration. I had intended to do it ; I have had many applications along this line from the employees of the canal and I have promised myself an opportunity of personally scrutinizing the paylists of the several canals and looking thoroughly into the question.
I am afraid the minister does not yet understand. He seems to think they are paid $1.50 a day. They are paid $45 a month.
And they work 30 days.

That is all right as an argument. They are paid $45 a month, and are paid by the month, that would be $1.50 a day if they worked 30 days. I was 239
quite correct in what I said. Assuming that they work 26 days they get 14| cents an hour. If they work 30 days, they would be getting a little less per hour and my argument would be all the stronger.
I pointed out to my hon. friend that in that item the Welland and Soo canals were especially exempted.

That is no answer at all. These locktenders make an application, and a statute is passed. Does the minister intend to tell this House and the country that he can explain away a statute by something said in this House. Does he think any judge will overrule a statute because of something which appears in ' Hansard ? ' The minister is shirking the question ; there is a statute providing for an increase of 25 cents a day for a different set of people altogether from those with whom the minister is dealing. I thought I made it clear that I was not talking about labourers. They get the same wage all over the canal system. The minister wants to make this House believe, perhaps he himself believes that it is for the labourers I am making application. I think I said distinctly that it was for the lockmasters, the locktenders and the bridge keepers, those mentioned in the statutes that I was applying. No one disputes that the labourers on the Welland canaj had their wages increased a few years ago, but the wages of the lock-masters. locktenders, and bridge tenders were not increased, and these men are now getting the same wages as they got on the very first day the new Welland canal was opened. They have never had an increase in that period of some 25 years. The labourers having obtained an increase a few years ago were getting a better rate of pay last year than on the other canals and that was equalized. But that is not the statute. This statute deals specifically with the very men on whose behalf I am applying. It deals with the lockmasters, bridge tenders and ferry men, not the labourers at all, unless under the general acceptation of the word that all men who work are labourers. These men get $45 a month as they have done ever since the new canal was opened.
That statute provides for an increase of 25 cents per day in the wages of lock-masters, lockmen. bridgemen and ferrymen on the canals of Canada generally. The minister has not told us how he gets round that statute. I do not care what ' Hansard ' may show that anybody said as to what the intention was. Here is the statute which we have to go by, passed after the supplementary estimates were brought down, and it is worded exactly as the supplementary estimates were. I was satisfied that if the supplementary estimates went through as brought down, these men on the Welland canal would get what they wanted ; and the minister will not say that I was foolish

enough, on behalf of these men, not to let well enough alone. The statute was passed, it became the lawr of the land, and the minister has not attempted to tell me yet how he can justify his failure to pay those men the increase mentioned in that statute. The statute applies to all the canals in Canada ; the Welland canal is one of those canals, and if the increase is not to be paid to the men on the Welland canal, there is no more authority for paying it on the Soulanges canal or the Lachine canal. The ordinary labourers on the Welland canal had their :pay increased a few years ago. They are not included in the item of the statute, -and they do not come within the description -of the men on whose behalf I have been ..pleading for the increase for two years, and to whom the statute applies. I *can assure the minister that his saying that it was never intended to be given to *these men will not satisfy them. The statute has been passed to apply to them, and if it does not apply to them, to whom does it apply ? I suppose the increase of 25 cents a day amounting to $37,000 has been paid to somebody. I do not suppose it was appropriated by this parliament to be withheld. If it has been paid to anybody, I want to know, on behalf of these men on the Welland canal, why it has not been paid to them. If that money has been paid Ho other lockmen on other canals, the ain blister must give some better explanation than he has yet given as to why he has not paid the increase of 25 cents a day to the Welland canal employees, who, it seems to me are entitled as a matter of law to have that increase from this government by the terms of last year's statute.

Has the Minister of Railways done anything towards granting the request as to which I have had considerable correspondence with the department, in reference to the old canal bank at Lachine ? The citizens have requested the government to give them a lease of the bank in order that they may convert it into a pleasure ground. The government cannot lose anything by acceding to their request and I believe my hon. friend was favourable to granting it. Some time ago I mentioned the matter to him and he said it would be attended to in a few days. That was nearly a month ago and the summer is far advanced, and I hope he will see his way clear to granting this request. It is a small matter for the government, they do not stand to lose anything by it, and it will be a considerable advantage to the locality.

The matter has been Tinder consideration but is not one that can be settled off hand. There must of necessity be a lease, and that lease must be authorized by the Governor in Council, and there is such a congestion of work before that body that this item has been lost sight 'Mr. LANCASTER.
of. However, I hope to be able to state shortly, as representing the department, the position in which the department is placed as regards that matter.
What are the lockmas-ters getting on the canal ?
$45 per month.

The other evening we had a dispute as to the number of locks on the Farran's Point canal. I wrote a gentleman at Farran's Point, and he replied that there was only one lock. I also inquired from a pilot who came through the canal the other day, and he gave the same information, but on page W-74 of the Auditor General's Report I find that on lock 22 there is a lockmaster and three men. I would like to know where that other lock is or. that Farran's Point canal.

There is a new lock, and right alongside of that is the old lock. Personally, I know nothing about it, but I am informed by the reports of the department and the officials and the chief engineer that there are two locks there. Some body is under a wrong impression, and I would be sorry to think it is the Chief Engineer of Railways and Canals.

Does this item cover the salary of the ornamental gentleman who is supposed to be superintendent of these different canals ? I am referring to a gentleman named Stewart, who was a short time ago the Liberal organizer in the county of Glengarry.
That is very much to his credit.
It may be to his credit, but I do not know where he learned anything about canals when organizing the Liberal party in the county of Glengarry.
He must have been watching the other side.

Although he had no experience, he was put in a position over men who have had a lifelong experience in that work. What is he receiving now ? I would ask also whether the government have given him possession of the little steamer called the ' Alert,' formerly controlled by Mr. Ru-bidge, late engineer in chief of canals ? Mr Stewart is now moving about the river fron canal to canal with this steamer. I think it has only a crew of half a dozen men, and probably does not add to the expenses of the country over $50 a day, but it does seem a little expensive for Mr. Stewart, who formerly could take a horse and carriage and go along the banks of the canals. Has this boat been handed over to him for his pleasure travel during the season of navigation, or is it to be retained for the engineer in chief ? Or for what purpose is this steamer to be used ? I have yet to see that it has ever served any useful purpose. Its only purpose seemed to be to give

pleasure to a very worthy man, the late chief engineer.
Mr. EMMERiSON. That matter was discussed very fully this afternoon, and had my hon. friend been present I would have been spared the necessity of repeating what I then said. The steamer ' Alert ' has been under the superintending engineer, Mr. ltu bidge. He used it in connection with his duties on the canals. Unfortunately, that gentleman passed away and, pending a final decision as to whether the steamer was necessary on the canal or not, it was placed superintendent of the Cornwall canal who also has charge of all the other plant and material in connection with the canals. If it was necessary for the engineers on those canals before the death of Mr. Rubidge, t assume it would be necessary for them to use it now. I have not had opportunity of personally finding out , what is necessary there, but when I do have that opportunity I will determine whether it is necessary to continue the boat at all in connection with the canal. If the facts be as stated by my hon. friend, who probably has coloured them somewhat, it would not be wise to continue it. The superintendent has charge of the Cornwall and Williamsburgli canals, which are-separated by quite a number of miles, and the engineers are still there. They will be required, probably, in connection with certain works not yet completed, to visit different points, and the steamer is at their disposal for that purpose.

Why is it necessary t-j have half a dozen superintendents at present when these canals were formerly managed with a far less number ? Take the Cornwall canal, which is one of the largest. In former years there was a superintendent receiving $1,400 a year. To-day we have a superintendent of the Cornwall canal who is called an overseer. Then we have an overseer of the Willlamsburgh canal and an overseer of the Edwardsburg canal, and above them all is Mr. Stewart as superintendent. The expenses have practically trebled in the last few years. I would also like to put another question. We have another gentleman down there called O'Callaghan. I do not know just what his position is, but I know he is a farmer, and he spends all his time on his farm. He has a very nice little farm a short distance from the town, where he spends all his time except when he comes in to draw his salary from this government.
He is of no assistance whatever to the party whom he is supposed to assist, for he is never there. From early morning till late at night, I am informed, he is engaged attending to his farming duties, and only comes up to draw his pay. That is only one instance. I find signs there of an approaching election. When I go home I find men by the score employed on the banks of the canal. All a man has to do is go to the gentleman who has received the nomination as standard bearer of the Liberal party, 239J
and he gets employment. I do not know what these men do, but I am told that they are engaged in pulling weeds and drawing their salaries. I assume that they are supposed to vote right when the election comes on. But, seriously, I would draw attention to Mr. O'Callaghan's case. I am speaking from information given me by reliable parties.
What position does he hold ?
I cannot just tell.
The hon. gentleman's information must be very inadequate.

All I know is that he is engaged in farming and drawing his pay from the government. What particular position he is supposed to hold or what he is supposed to do, I have no means of knowing. 1 suppose the deputy minister could tell the hon. gentleman what he is supposed to do. For my part I never saw him do anything. Surely, the hon. minister might tell me-
I did not wish to be discourteous and interrupt my hon. friend (Mr. Pringle).
Very well, tell me what he is supposed to do.

One man is employed there as collector for the day service. Mr. O'Callaghan is the night man, and the reason my hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) does not see him there is because the hon. gentleman is not there at night. I am afraid that my hon. friend's remarks are tinged with extravagance and not altogether free from bitterness. due to the fact that Mr. Stewart and the other gentleman were at oue time identified with the Liberal party. He should not harbour resentment against them on that account. I think it is to their credit that they were Liberals and I do not think that they should be misrepresented in the House because of that fact.
Perhaps the hon. minister will -allow me to say that Mr. O Callaghan was always supposed to be a Conservative.
That shows how fair we are
It shows how fair I am. He was appointed at the instance of the late Dr. Bergin.

I think it is an example of our fairness. Were we actuated by the bitterness shown by my hon. friend, if this man does nothing but draw his pay how quickly we could get rid of him. And surely my hon. friend does not wish the committee to understand that the men employed on the banks of the canal are employed in pulling weeds. Surely he knows-what is the fact-that these men are employed on the stone lining of the banks of the canal.

The hon. gentleman admits that his information is very inaccurate. It is shadowy, so to speak. He is depending entirely upon hearsay, and somebody has been telling him things that were not in accordance with the facts.
Will the hon. minister tell me how many of these men are employed on the rip-rapping at the present time ? The number has increased very largely during the last three weeks.
The number of men varies. My officers cannot tell me the number of men.
I suppose the number varies as the election approaches.	,
If that were in mind, it would be better to ' bide a wee.'
The hon. minister will see that there are others along the St. Lawrence canal who have noticed the fact of Mr. Stewart having taken possession of the steamer ' Alert.'

He is the superintendent of these canals, and the ste'amer .* Alert ' has been placed in his charge as has the rest of the plant. The hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) says there are three overseers. As a matter of fact there are only two, one on the Williamsburgh canal and one on the Cornwall canal. These canals are ten or twelve miles apart, and it is necessary to have officials of this class at each canal.
Now, let me tell the minister the position. In the old days there was a superintendent at Cornwall and one at Morrisburg.
And the superintending engineer.

And the superintending engineer, the late Mr. Rubidge. These superintendents made out their reports themselves and sent them to Ottawa. They had plenty of time to do it. They had only to drive up and down the canal, one day east and the next day west. Shortly after this government came into power they passed an Order in Council abolishing the position of superintendents of canals, so as to get rid of these men.
The hon. gentleman is imagining that.

Not at all. One of them was Dr. Hickey, for many years a member of this House, and the other was Mr. Ross. The hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) can corroborate what I state. And shortly after the government decided to have overseers. And they not only have two overseers but they have another gentleman whom they call clerk to the overseer. I think the hon. member for Cornwall will say that there is an officer of that kind there.

At all events, we have one on the Williamsburgh canal. So, instead of having two men they have three and I think even four men on this canal, besides Mr. Stewart. Now, this boat has been given to Mr. Stewart to run up and down the canal. The minister states that she will be used by the engineers on the different works as heretofore. But is it not a fact that all these works are completed, and is it not also a fact that even if these works existed, the engineer on one of these works would have nothing to do with another ? There is no way that they can use this boat. It is a well known fact that this boat is absolutely of no use, yet it involves an expenditure to this country of $8,000 or $10,000 per annum. But on account of Mr. Rubidge having been connected with the canals for thirty years or forty years, there was not the same general fault finding that there is now since it has been handed over to Mr. Stewart to be left in his charge without being used.
Is there any jealousy in connection with it V

No jealousy whatever ; but the people of this country expect the Minister of Railways to manage their affairs as economically as they ought to be managed, having due regard to the country's interests.

I do not think the Minister of Railways should talk of jealousy. It is public money that he has control pf, and not his own. 1 want to tell the minister that the editor of the Brighton ' Ensign ' announced that this government steamer was up at Twelve O'clock Point in East Northumberland, and Mr. Stewart's family was on board the steamer. I suppose the country is paying the board of that gentleman and his family on board the steamer while they are on a pleasure trip to Twelve O'clock Point, at the head of the Bay of Quinte. There was not any jealousy in the breast of the editor of the Brighton [DOT] Ensign ' when he announced that fact; neither is there any jealousy in my mind be cause I object to the government paying out the people's money for the board of this gentleman and his family on that steamer. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that it comes with bad grace for him to talk about jealousy in view of the fact that every man was turned off the Murray canal when his party got into power. I give as much credit to Liberals of the county of East Northumberland who represented that riding in past years, as I give to Conservatives, because up to the time this government came into power no government official was ever turned out of his position in that riding by Mr. Biggar, the Reform representative. Men died in their public positions who were appointed by Mr. Mackenzie's Liberal government. But when this so-called Liberal government came

into power they were so low in their minds that they turned men oft' that canal because they were Conservatives. Every man who was a Conservative was turned off that canal. They turned men out of houses that they built themselves on the authority of the government, and this fact can be verified by the deputy minister who is now sitting by the bon. gentleman ; and they put their Grit friends into their positions and into these houses that had been vacated. and gave them $C a month, whereas they had only paid the men who owned the houses $3 a month. That is the way they conduct business in East Northumberland. What does the superintendent of that canal want with an inspector over him ? The superintendent of that canal was a purchaser of cheese, and knows nothing about canal work. The minister is paying the superintendent a salary, and giving him $6 a mouth for a house, and $6 a month for office rent, and he is paying him $1.50 for each one of 255 trips to the Murray canal. That is the way they work it, Mr. Chairman, and I know your soul must be grieved in hearing of the extravagance of your party. Just think of the superintendent of the Murray canal living in Brighton in a house that the government pays rent for and au office that the government pays rent for, and then they give him $1.50 each for 255 trips to go down to the Murray canal to attend to liis business. Then they give him $2 a trip to go down to Trenton at the eastern end of the Murray canal, and when he takes a jaunt into the country they pay him $2 or $3 a day for that. And the Minister of Railways talks about jealousy 1 I want to tell him that I am here to look after the people's money and the way it is expended, and that is the venom that was in their bosoms when they turned poor men off that canal and put in their own friends.

Before that item is carried I want to draw the minister's attention to another matter that I think is a grievance, and that is in regard to the pension of these lock tenders and lockmasters upon the Welland canal. I think in common fairness the minister ought to revise the system of superannuation as it is ap-lied to these men on the Welland canal. As the minister mentioned a few minutes ago, these men are employed sometimes on extra work on the canal ; by virtue of their being lockmasters they are given the first preference when this extra work presents itself. Now they get that money just as much because they are lock tenders as they do their $45 a month salary; but they are not allowed to include that in the computation of their superannuation. It seems to me that their contention that they do not get the right amount of superannuation is a fair and just one. Take for example the case of Mr. Henry Hare, whose case I think his
deputy is acquainted with. I have in my hand a letter from Mr. Ij. K. Jones, the secretary of the department, to Mr. Hare, written on the 29th of January last, and here is what Mr. Jones writes :
I am directed to inform you, as desired, that your pay for the three fiscal years pre-ceeding your superannuation, as returned in the pay sheets upon which you paid deduction was as follows :	1900,	$350.10 ;	1901,
$351.35 ; 1902, $353.07, making an avrage fori three years of $351.50.
The minister will remember that I was quite 11415111 the mark in saying that the locktenders did not get more than $360 a year and there is the case of a man working all the time who only got an average of $351.50. Now Mr. Jones goes on to say :
Your view that you are entitled to further-superannuation allowance on the amount paid to you for certain services in regard of water "level record during the winter, and the superannuation reduction should have been made from it, is a mistaken one.
The department could, had it seen fit, have employed any parties outside of the ordinary canal staff to do this particular work, and you surely would not contend that such parties would be entitled to superannuation allowance on the pay given therefor.
As a matter of convenience and advantage to the lock-tenders, they were allowed to look after this work of level taking, and were paid for it as any outsider might have been. It has nothing to do with their regular employment or regular pay, which last is a clearly defined monthly rate.
What I submit to the hon. minister is that it is because the men are lock tenders they have this extra work for a few weeks in the year. They are employed as any other persons might possibly have been but they are given the preference over an outside party because they are lock tenders. I think it is a fair contention that if a lock tender got that amount of money which he would not have got unless he had been officially in the capacity of a lock tender the govr eminent should take that into consideration in making their computation as to his superannuation. These men would not have got that money but for the fact that they were lock tenders and they did get it because they were lock tenders. They are given the preference and I think it is reasonable to suppose that these men who for eight months in theJ year are in the employ of the government will do better work in level taking than an ordinary labourer casually picked up and who would not take as much interest in the government service. I think in striking the superannuation allowance, as Mr. Hare contended, the fact of his having received this money should be taken into consideration, because, although it is true that this money is not part of his lock tender's wage, he would not 1 have received this extra money if lie had not

been a lock tender and it is therefore fair to take the three years added to his lock tender's wages in computing the amount of his superannuation allowance. He gets it from the government the same as he receives his wage as an employee on the Welland canal and he receives it because he is a canal employee. He would not have received it had he not been in a permanent position and I submit to the Minister of Railways and Canals that this fact should be taken into consideration in the future. The case which I am now instancing has been dealt with and I will not ask the hon. minister to overrule what has been decided. In this particular case it would do no good because Mr. Hare died since this session began. He died two or three months ago. His case is common to all of these men and I am using it as an illustration. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether it would not be reasonable to include in the amount that you strike for superannuation all that these men receive for the three years from the government whether it be their regular salary as lock tenders or any additional amount.

This is a matter that is controlled by the treasury board and it is decided in accordance with the interpretation of the Act. It is the permanent pay which the men get which is taken into account. It is true that it has been deemed advisable to give these men extra pay. That perhaps is an Act of grace but it is not in connection with their permanent employment. However, this is not a matter for the department. It is a matter that is determined under the law by the Treasury Board.

I would like an answer to the question that I brought the hon. minister's attention to. What is the hon. minister's idea about paying a man for 250 days to attend to his work at $1.50 a day when he gets a salary for doing that business ?

The gentleman to whom my hon. friend refers is paid in the usual way for the travelling that he does in connection with his duties on the canals. I think perhaps my hon. friend is looking at the matter through a glass darkly.

I think the hon. minister is looking through a glass darkly. Are we to understand that this government employs a man, bring him up from another part of the riding altogether and instead of insisting on him living where it is not out of the way at all, because there are beautiful residences all along the canal, residences that a good many of us would be very glad to have, pay for the rent of a house and office in the village of Brighton for the use of this official ? Are we to understand that the government are willing to pay Mr. LANCASTER.
out the people's money for this official if he wants to run down the canal to attend to his business ? If he wants to go to Trenton they give him $2 a day and if he wants to go out into the country on an excursion to the old village where he used to live they give him $2 a day of the people's money.

I would like to say one word with regard to this ornamental gentleman-Mr. Stewart. I am a little surprised at the attitude which the hon. minister takes in standing up for Mr. Stewart in connection with the use of his pleasure yacht. I find in the accounts of last year many items charged by Mr. Stewart. They are only small items and I do not care about taking up the time of the committee by reading them all-$106 for travelling expenses and so forth. I find that last year he was in the habit of charging the government for tips, wines_ and hotel bills at the Place Viger. This is a purely ornamental official of no use at all, who knows no more about the canals than a mere schoolboy and who has simply been put over the [DOT] heads, of the men who have been employed for years upon the canals because he rendered good service to the Liberal Party. I would like to see this man treated generously, but I draw the line when he has a yacht placed at his disposal and has four or five men tu take him up and down the river and who runs up hotel bills at the Place Viger and charges his wines and tips to the government. I think the line should be drawn and that Mr. Stewart should be called down and instructed to perform his duties if you sent him away a hundred miles from the canal it would be better for the canal and for the government. But, if you are going to keep him there let him conduct his services without imposing such an enormous expense upon the country. It is time to cut off the steam yacht and these extra expenses which we see here in the Auditor General's Report.

I would like to ask the hon. minister how it is that the pay of the men, employed on the Lachine canal was delayed until the 18th July. My hon. friend cannot imagine what a very great inconvenience and hardship it is for these men to wait eighteen days for their pay. These men in the city of Montreal and along the whole length of the canal are poor men, they work hard and that they have to wait for eighteen days for their pay, seems to be a very great injustice if it cannot be absolutely ex* plained. While the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) was giving us a tableau of Mr. Stewart living like aliabob, and this other gentleman Mr. O'Callaghan, leading the life of a gentleman farmer, issuing from his house only on pay day, it seems almost a sin that those who are really at work, who are not, to use my hon. friend's expression, ornemental political employees, the hardworking men employed in and near great

cities, should have to wait eighteen days for their pay. I refrained from calling the minister's attention to this earlier, but I have since July 18th many complaints and I think it is only due to these men that my hon. friend should give some explanation of this delay.

A number of men have been employed lately in connection with the Cornwall canal. Their pay is long overdue and some of them came	to me in reference to their
pay, asking when this government were likely to pay their wages. I told them it was impossible for me to say, that probably after the session was over they would find time to attend to the payment. These men can ill-aiford to wait for months for their pay. There should be some means by which they would be paid at once.

Before replying to these questions I wish to call attention to the way misstatements are made in this House and circulated. My hon. friend stated as a rumour that a certain gentleman worked in the daytime on his farm and drew his pay. I called his attention to the fact that that man was employed at night and that that duty required him to attend to the canal at night and that he was paid for that.
Collecting when there is nothing to collect.

It is not the collection. His duties require him to attend at night. The daytime is free to him and he can be at his farm. That is the first misstatement I corrected, and my hon. friend repeated it as if it had not been corrected. There was a delay in paying the men on the Lachine canal during the month of June. The pay lists came up, they had to be checked over and had to be sent back to be corrected. They came back again and then they had to be checked over and then sent to the Auditor General who also had to check them over. By the time all of this wheel has revolved, it is generally the 15th of the month and that is the time these payments are usually made. With respect to the Lachine canal, there has been an extra delay for three days. That has been the procedure for a long, long time ; it is not peculiar to the present.

I do not agree with my hon. friend as to that. The delay on the Lachine canal could not have been as short as that or I would not have had these representations made to me. As to the collectorship, the minister said, in answer to the hon. member for Cornwall, that this singularly fortunate individual whose name is O'Callaghan, had night work as a collector, but we all know the collections on the canal have been abolished since last year-that is one of the boasts of the government-and if Mr. O'Callaghan is as busy collecting as the officials on the Lachine have been since the tolls were abolished, he must work at night to have such a defence as the minister liajs set up for him.

The minister has not explained one item, the wines for Mr. Stewart. I am sure it will harrow the soul of that apostle of temperance, the minister of Agriculture the late general of the Canadian army, and I am sure the minister should state who the parties are who allowed Mr. Stewart to be furnished with wines and will prevent its being done in the future.
I asked the) deputy about this and he said there could not be any such charge, that it would not pass the department. I know nothing more of the circumstances than that.

I did not make the charge in ignorance of what I was talking about. If the minister will take the accounts of the Place Viger Hotel as against Mr. Stewart at the different times Mr. Stewart has been attending to Cornwall canal business in the Place Viger in Montreal he will find that Mr. Stewart was charged for wines, that he paid for them and that the government recouped him for them.

I am free to say that if such a payment was made it was improper and incorrect, and was not in accord with the wishes of the department. I have spoken to the deputy who said that it was not possible and if anything of the kind has been allowed, is was through the inadvertence of the accountants.

It is a very, very small item and probably I should not have called attention to it, but the item goes with the man. Mr. Stewart has been putting in bills year after year including all the expenses he could have at the hotels, charging his tips, wines and everything, and the government have been paying them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an understanding with my hon. friends opposite and I now desire that the committee would be good enough to suspend operations for a short time in order that I may bring down some important documents. With the understanding that the committee will return to its labours by consent in a few minutes, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
Some resolution^ reported.

subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR GENERAL-SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.
MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR GENERAL-SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.
speechtext: FIELDING (Minister of Finance) presented a message from His Excellency the Governor General.
Motion agreed to.

House in Committee of Supply.
Canals-salaries and contingencies, collectors' offices, $35,835.
There is an increase in this item over last year.
There is a net increase of $110, which occurs in contingencies.
How does the minister increase this expenditure when it has been stated that there are no collections on the canals ?

We have to keep the officials just the same, in order to keep the record and pending the two years experiment.
Galops Rapids-to complete channel, $40,000.

I brought down to the house last week copies of the contracts relating to the Galops rapids. The documents were placed by me on the table, and some of the hon. gentlemen opposite got them. I would like to ask if any lion, gentleman has them ? I thought they were obtained by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox.

I may say that I have been trying all afternoon to find out where they are, and no member on this side of the House acknowledges having seen them, the clerk says he never saw them, and they are not upstairs, where papers of this kind are generally to be found. For that reason I think it would be most unfair to press this item until we have an opportunity of seeing the documents which my hon. friend promised.

If we pass this item, it will finish the main estimates, and there is an item in the supplementary estimates for the Galops rapids on which the matter can be fully discussed, and I will have the information copied again and furnished to my hon. friend to-morrow morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. ,T. D. REID. Of course, I think it is unfair to ask that this item pass without my having an opportunity to see the papers. The minister may bring the supplementary estimates on at some moment when I am not here, and I may not have the opportunity of discussing this matter again.
My hon. friend can rest assured that as long as I am in this House I will not take any course of that character with respect to the estimates under my control.

If the hon. minister will state that there is an item in the supplementary estimates for the Galops rapids, and that it will not be pressed through without my having an opportunity to discuss it, I am quite willing to let this item go.

There is in the supplementary estimates an item for the Galops rapids, and my hon. friend will have that opportunity, and I will put myself out to accommodate him as to the time when it will be discussed.
Building a spur line of railway from Intercolonial station at RiviSre Ouelle to wharf on the St. Lawrence-balance, $6,300.
How long is that ?
Seven miles.
Is that built specially for the use of the government road or some other purpose 1 Has not somebody built a mill there, and does he not require that road to haul lumber ?

No ; it is to connect the RiviSre Ouelle wharf with the ferry at Murray Bay. It is built for the benefit of the Murray Bay traffic.
Intercolonial Railway-St. Charles Junction -bore hole for water supply, $4,750.

We had to get water there. The Intercolonial was very much inconvenienced last year for want of water. This amount was expended because of the depth.
Intercolonial Railway - Campbellton-siding on wharf at, $1,250.

It was necessary to put in a siding there. There is a large wharf at that place.
Intercolonial Railway-Sussex-platform extension at military siding, $950.

That is where the militia drill. They have their permanent military establishment there, and the platform was furnished for the benefit of the military. [DOT]
Intercolonial Railway-Spring Hill Junction- -bore hole for water supply, $2,800.
Could no water be got tliere without boring for it ?
No ; this was absolutely necessary.
Are there not a number of hills there ?

There may be, but this boring for water was the last resort.
Intercolonial Railway-siding at Pietou Landing, $14,500.
This work was given under contract after tender, and the lowest tender was taken.
Is that the matter about which there was some discussion last year ?

I think not. This arises out of the shipment of coal. The wharf had been raised by the coal companies and there had to be a different grade, so that the grades go down one way and up the other. This siding became necessary on account of the grades.
A sort of switchback ?
Yes.
That is on the New Glasgow side, opposite the town of Pietou ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is Pietou landing, where the coal is shipped from the Acadia mines.
I would like to ask the minister if it is time now to talk about the question I asked this afternoon ?

Item 91 of the main estimates has been held over, so that my hon. friend will have an opportunity to discuss the question on that item. I did not press it, because the hon. member for West Toronto said that when it came up he wished, to be present.
Lachine canal-electric generator, electric cables and shafting, $5,000.
Is that a new machine V
That is the balance on the work of the new gates put in on the Lachine canal.
What is the total cost of all these ?
I have not the figures just now.
The minister seems to be rather short of information.

I have sent for the information, and I shall have it in a few minutes. Let the item stand in the meantime.
Item allowed to stand.
Railways and canals-chargeable to income- Lachine canal-repairs to old locks, 1 and 2, $25,000.
Will the minister please give us some explanation of this ?,
We have had to repair the old locks 1 and 2 of the Lachine canal, and this $25,000 is required to meet the expenditure made for the fiscal year ending 30th June, 1904.
Was this work let by tender ?
Yes.
Who had the contract ?
Quinlin & Robinson.
By the yard ?
By schedule. The contract was let to the lowest tenderer.
Was it publicly advertised.	*

Yes, generally advertised.
Lachine canal-tail race, Cote St. Paul, $3,956.10.
Was anything ever done about that basin near Montreal that the government own and that was used for a dry-dock ?

The Tate dry-dock. It is leased to Mr. L'Etand for $1,000 a year he making the ordinary repairs. But it is found necessary to rebuild that dry-dock, and there is an item in the supplementary estimates for that purpose.
Is it understood that this gentleman will have the lease still at SI,000 per annum ?
If we continue the lease the terms will have to be arranged ? It may be that the terms will have to be increased.
What is the amount in the supplementary estimates ?
Speaking from memory the estimate of the total cost is $10,000. If we get $1,000, that will be 10 per cent on the investment.
I do not think there would be any trouble in leasing it for $1,000 a year now, aud let the lessee put on the repairs. It is a nice dry-dock for vessels running on the I.achine canal.
It is small.
It takes in small canal boats and it is the only place at which they can be docked, unless they go to Quebec.

We can discuss the matter when the item is before us.
Lachine canal-water service for protection against fire, $1,800.
Where is that ?

This is to lay an eight inch pipe from the city water works

main on Mill street to the north side of the dry-dock, 650 feet where a hydrant will be placed. The canal fleet is put in the dock each winter and there are a number of buildings and also a considerable quantity of material for lock gates &c, without protection against fire. The value of the fleet dredges, tugs, &c., is about $100,000.

They are placed in the dry dock you have just leased ? I would like to know also if the government have to pay any charges for their vessels being taken out in the dry-dock, or if that point was reserved in the lease that was made ?

No, we do not pay anything.
Lachine canal-raising shed No. 1, St. Gabriel Basin, $10,000.
This is done to meet the shipping requirements. The work was advertised and put up for tender.
Who got the contract ?
A man named Quinlan. I would like to reduce that amount to $8,000, because we will not spend more than $8,000, and the balance is provided for in the supplementaries for the current year.
Motion agreed to.
What is the amount of Quinlan's tender ?
I cannot give the exact figure.
How many tenders did you receive ?
Three tenders and this was the lowest.

In every other department when we ask for this information it is generally given. I think we should know the names of the tenderers and the amounts, because the public in that vicinity are curious to know these things, and to see whether the lowest tender was accepted.
In other words, whether I was telling the truth or not.
Not for that reason, but because they like to know the difference there was between the tenders.
I would be sorry if, when I stated that a certain tender was the lowest, any doubt would still exist in the minds of the committee.

I do not wish the minister to take my request in that sense at all, I do not dispute his word. But I think it is fair that we should have this information. It has been shown in this House that the lowest tender has not always been accepted.

I should be sorry if that were the case. If the lowest tender had not been accepted in this case, then I think Mr. EMMERSON.
it would be desirable for the minister to come prepared with a detailed statement showing -why the lowest tender was not accepted. But I fail to see why it is necessary to bring forward voluminous information to show why the lowest tender was accepted. Tenders were publicly asked, a certain number were received, and the department accepted the lowest.

In items of this kind it is generally expected that the minister will have the names of the tenderers and the amount. Here is a vote for $10,000, and the minister says he has no information whatever as to who the tenderers were and the amounts, and he asks us to vote it blind.
If my hon. friend will allow the item to go through I will furnish him with a statement in the morning. I agree with him that the information should be furnished.

Sometimes these promises are not very well fulfilled after the item goes through. The hon. gentleman will be good enough to see that the information is produced. There is nothing to spur a minister's memory after the item has gone through.

That has not occurred in connection with my estimates.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. I am not speaking of the present minister, I am speaking of all ministers. They do not take so much interest in getting the information about an item once it has passed. Therefore, if this item is passed we will expect that full information to-morrow morning without fail.

I will bring it tomorrow morning without fail.
Lachine canal-lock gates, $30,000.

This amount is required to build four new lock gates, they were to have been completed before the 30th of June, 1904. This is a supplementary vote. They are being built by employees of the department under the direction of the superintendent.
Does this come under the head of repairs ?

It is for repairs, it is not a capital expenditure. These gates are for locks 1 and 2, which are being rebuilt.
Chambly canal-to complete waste weir at electric power house, $2,500.

This is for a waste weir at the electric power house. The present weir is a wooden structure built twenty years ago. It is proposed to make one of concrete. Most of the materials are on hand having been purchased out of the appropriation voted last year for this work and another weir at Ste. Therese island. When the present one is completed it will only

leave a couple of wooden weirs on the canal, it is the intention to build them of concrete entirely.
Has the government a powerhouse there ?
Yes.
This is in connection with a government owned power-house and has no reference to any electrical power company there ?

None whatever.
Chambly canal-damage by flooding, $1,736.
In connection with this item I would like to ask the hon. minister who are the parties to he indemnified and what is the amount to be given to each ?

The award was made by Marcelin Robert. This was for damages caused by the overflowing of a culvert under the canal. The persons to whom damages have been awarded, and the amounts are as follows :

Coupal	 50
Joseph Dupois, pSre	200
Octave Poirier	 200
Julien Audette	 25
J. B.. Many	300
Lewis Dupuis	,	350
Jean Baptiste Sapaline, dit Gaboriau .. .. 310

Edward Chartier	400
Marcelin Robert (valuator)	 61
Is this amount intended to cover all the damages caused by flooding ?
All the damages caused by flooding from the culvert under the canal.
Has this sum any reference whatever to damages caused by flooding by the building of a dam there for the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company ?
No. Two items stood over in regard to which there will be no discussion but in regard to which some information was wanted and while I have it here possibly there will be no objection to them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Bring it down to-morrow.
There are only these two items, and if there is to be any discussion I certainly will accede to the hon. gentleman's request.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What are they ?

There is item 27 :
Lachine canal-electric generator, electric cable and shafting, $5,000.
Carried.

Then, there is the item :
Lachine canal-enlargement and improvement, $24,000.
I want to take that out of the estimates for 1903-4 because it will be found in the supplementary estimates for the current year. I therefore beg to move that the item be struck out.
Motion agreed to.

The next item is :
Lachine canal

construction and equipment (revote), $62,000.
I beg to move to reduce that item from $62,000 to $57,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is it for ?

This is to provide for the construction of workshops at Cascades Point. The work is under contract and was completed in June, 1904. It is also to pay the balance due on the final estimates of R. McDonald and of the Canadian General Electric Company under their contracts. The whole amount is $62,000 but as there are only $57,000 of it paid out of the 1903-4 appropriation we are asking for that sum to be voted and the balance of $5,000 will be provided for in the supplementary estimates for the current year.

Motion agreed to.
Soulanges canal-land and land damages, $650.

This is to indemnify landowners for past damages for land taken at Bissonette's Gully. There are $3,000 in the main estimates for widening and deepening this gully and there will be no further damage by flooding.
Cornwall canal-strengthening and protecting north bank, &c., $5,600.
I beg to move to reduce that item to $2,600.
That had better stand.
This is by arrangement.

I understood that the Cornwall - canal item in the main estimates stood. Is that correct ?
Mr. EMME(RSON. No. It was rearranged that those items were to be passed through in order to expedite the business of the House, and that the discusssion would arise on the supplementary estimates.
I have been here most of the time, and I have heard nothing of the kind.
It was this evening ; my hon. friend could not have been in the House.

With whom was the arrangement made ? There are certain members who have charge of that matter and it was very distinctly understood that the

Cornwall canal item was to stand for dis-cusion of the Davis contract.
So it does.
It should not have been passed to-night.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is not passed.
There is confusion somewhere.

The understanding was that there should be an opportunity for the discussion of that contract, and in the Sup-plementaries for this year there will be found a further amount and the discussion may be had upon it.
I have been here all evening and 1 did not hear of any such bargain.

I said that the two items, the Cornwall canal and the Galops Rapids, were to pass with the consent of hon. members and that the discussion which was desired in connection with the Davis contract and also upon the contracts in connection with the Galops Rapids should take place under the supplementary items referring to those two canals.

We can shorten this matter. easily. It was distinctly understood the other day when the matter was partly discussed by the Minister of Justice that this item would stand in order to get certain papers and unless the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) or myself had made an arrangement it should not have been passed. We have charge of this matter and we do not propose that the main item for the Cornwall canal shall pass until after that, item is discussed. We have our own reasons for not wishing it to depend on supplementaries and I would ask to have that item considered as standing over as arranged the other day.
The hon. leader of the opposition was in the House when the matter was talked over and I made the statement I am now making. Of course if there is any objection I want to be reasonable.

It was understood before the hon. the leader of the opposition left tonight that we had come to the end of the day's work and I think it is well to carry out our understanding of the matter. The item should certainly stand.
This item of the Cornwall canal ?
This whole thing.
The other was passed.
It should not have been passed.

If an hon. member is out of the House he cannot come back and Mr. LENNOX.
complain of what has been done. I do not think that is treating the House fairly.

I suppose my hon. friend understands that a member cannot always be in the House. In the absence of those who were known to have charge of this matter this item should not have been passed, and if it has been passed by mistake it should be reopened now.

The minister will remember that the hon. leader of the opposition was not in the House when the item passed. He came in just as we finished the discussion of the Galops, and the discussion was that if we allowed that item to go through we could discuss it on the supplementaries to-morrow.

They were coupled together in my remarks. My hon. friend knows that all the papers he asked for were brought down. Very recently he made a request for some other papers and they are being prepared and will be ready for him in the morning.
Some papers which were not on the tile but were referred to were asked for by us. and this morning when we came to look over them we found that certain papers were not included.
Perhaps we might go to the next item.
I think it is an open violation of the understanding reached the other day. It was well understood that this whole item should stand and that there should be a regular discussion.
We cannot allow the one to stand that has passed already.
The one that has been passed accidentally should be re-opened.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon.. friends' intention was to have a discussion might I suggest that we have an opportunity for that in the item of the later supplementa-ries touching the Cornwall canal. If the intention is to have a motion to strike out the item I realize that my suggestion would not meet his view.

It does not meet my view because in the discussion of the Davis contract we should be absolutely at large and at liberty to take whatever course we choose. Of course I am now speaking subject to whatever decision the leader of the opposition who I am glad to see has entered the chamber, may take and I shall be glad to concur in any suggestion he makes, but I myself think that we should be left absolutely at large in regard to that item and not confined to any particular course.

The item should not have been proposed at all until the papers were printed and furnished to the House A great many demands were made to the

House that the papers should be brought down.
If there is any misunderstanding, I am perfectly willing that it should be left over.

The minister suggested that the file was an enormous file, that it would be a great expense and waste of time to print all the papers, and he asked me to name three gentlemen to look over them. I did so, and these gentlemen spent a good deal of time going over the papers, collecting at least a few of them to be printed. I suppose they are being printed now.
I suppose that it was by inadvertence that the item was passed, and 1 think it should be re-opened.

I knew it was the desire to have these papers ; and, in order to expedite the business, I made the suggestion that these items of the main estimates be allowed to go through, and that the discussion would come up under the supplementary estimates of this year, which contain an item relating to the Cornwall canal. If there has been any misunderstanding, I am willing to let the item relating to the Cornwall canal stand.
We might as well let the other stand also, because I intend to divide the House on the Galops Rapids item.
My hon. friend will have an opportunity to divide the House on the other item.
I will let the item go through, but I wish to point out that it is an item which the Minister of Railways and Canals is trying to press through without, giving due justice to the House.

I am sorry my hon. friend is so uncharitable. My suggestion was only with a view of expediting business, not with the view of cutting off any discussion, or to prevent my hon. friend from saying what he pleases with respect to it. I move that item 93 in the main estimates- Cornwall canal, enlargement, $20,000-be reconsidered.

Motion agreed to.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.	[DOT]
What is the business for to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Justice will take up the Railway Bill, after which we will resume supply, with the estimates of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.
Tuesday, July 26, 1904.
